docs.title: Linux Setup
docs.text:
Assumptions:

  • You have installed X-Plane 11.50+
  • You have a reasonably fast CPU and broadband internet
  • FUSE is installed and setup (Enable user_allow_other in /etc/fuse.conf, if not already the case.)

docs.title: Steps:
docs.text:
1. Download the most recent packaged release (autortho_lin_####.bin) from here
  2. Make executable if needed chmod +x autoortho_lin.bin
  3. Run the program ./autoortho_lin.bin
  4. Configure your settings and paths for your system
  5. Download and setup an ortho set from the Scenery Library, or turn on scenery streaming to skip the download.
  6. Click Start Streaming
  7. Configure your scenery_packs.ini file appropriately
  8. Run X-Plane and choose a location for an ortho set you have downloaded

docs.title: Windows Setup
docs.text:
Assumptions:

  • You are running 64bit Windows 10+
  • You have install X-Plane 11.50+
  • You have setup and configured either: Dokan or WinFSP
    • If you have trouble with one, try the other! Some users on Windows 11 have better luck with WinFSP for some reason. Windows users should always attempt both before asking questions on forums!!!
    • If both Dokan and WinFSP are installed, Dokan will be preferred. Users can force preferring WinFSP by setting prefer_winfsp=True in their config file.
  • You install all components, including scenery, on a local NTFS drive.

docs.title: MacOS Setup
docs.text:
Assumptions:

  • You have installed X-Plane 11.50+
  • You have an Apple Silicon Computer (AutoOrtho Mac only supports arm64)
  • FUSE is installed, MacFuse and Fuse-T are supported.

docs.title: Steps:
docs.text:
1. If you haven't install MacFuse or Fuse-T. Fuse-T was used for testing the mac binary but both should work.
  2. Download the most recent packaged release (autortho_mac_####.zip) from here
  3. Unzip on the location you want.
  4. Run the program AutoOrtho.app

  5. Important: macOS Quarantine Warning - This program is currently unsigned. On first run, macOS will block it from opening. You have two options to fix this:

    Option A (Recommended): Remove the quarantine attribute using Terminal: bash xattr -d com.apple.quarantine /path/to/AutoOrtho.app Tip: You can drag the AutoOrtho.app onto the Terminal window to auto-fill the path.

    Option B: Use System Settings: - Go to Settings → Privacy and Security - Scroll down to find the message about AutoOrtho.app being blocked - Click Open Anyway

  6. Configure your settings and paths for your system

  7. Download and setup an ortho set from the Scenery Library, or turn on scenery streaming to skip the download.
  8. Click Start Streaming
  9. Configure your scenery_packs.ini file appropriately
  10. Run X-Plane and choose a location for an ortho set you have downloaded

docs.title: Requirements and Compatibility
docs.text:
To run from source, this project requires python3.x and all pre-requisites in the requirements.txt file. Also, a copy of X-Plane 11.50+ of course.

Most testing is done on Ubuntu 22.04 using FUSE. Other Linux flavors ought to work as well. MacOS very likely should work, but I have no way of testing it.

I have done testing on Windows 10 with the Dokan project. This does appear to work fine, but this is not how I use this project, so it's not my primary concern.

docs.title: Performance Features
docs.text: AutoOrtho includes advanced performance optimizations to minimize stuttering and reduce loading times:

docs.title: Native Pipeline (High Performance Mode)
docs.text:
AutoOrtho includes a native C pipeline that dramatically improves DDS texture building performance by bypassing Python's Global Interpreter Lock:

  • 10-20x faster DDS texture building
  • True multi-core parallelism via OpenMP
  • Native HTTP client with connection pooling for faster downloads

The native pipeline is automatically used when available. See the Performance Tuning Guide for details.

Note: Apple Maps downloads always use the Python HTTP client due to its special authentication requirements. Other imagery sources use the faster native client.

docs.title: Additional Features
docs.text:
• Spatial Prefetching: Downloads tiles ahead of your aircraft
  • SimBrief Integration: Uses your flight plan for smarter prefetching
  • Dynamic Zoom: Automatically adjusts quality based on altitude
  • Time Budget System: Predictable tile loading times

See the Performance Tuning Guide for configuration options.

docs.title: Known issues and limits
docs.text:
• Currently I try to limit the memory usage, though it's possible it will exceed this in certain scenarios.
  • Not really possible to post-process the satellite photos. You get what you get.
  • Will add a couple minutes to initial flight time for new areas. That's to be expected though.
  • Will require and use a lot of internet requests (surprise!) and writes a lot of small files locally. There are many parts along your path that may need tuning or may not like this (ISP, DNS, Wifi, drive speed, CPU speed, etc). User's should be ready to diagnose their specific setup and determine if this project fits withing their own personal computing requirements.
  • Windows has too many variations with how filesystems are handled, links are done, intrusive malware detection systems, etc and will likely always be slower and more difficult to use with this project.
  • Apple Maps always uses Python HTTP client (not native) due to special authentication requirements.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Setup and configuration for most use cases should be pretty simple. The important settings are:

  • Scenery install path
  • X-Plane install path
  • Downloader directory

docs.title: First-run setup
docs.text:
On a new installation, AutoOrtho opens a guided setup wizard that:

  1. Welcome and checks: the required FUSE backend for this platform.
  2. X-Plane: detected, or browse for it.
  3. Scenery: the scenery folder, whether to stream scenery, and regions to install (or use scenery you already have). Tick Stream scenery you haven't installed to fly without installing regions, or stream as well as install: installed regions are always used first. Choose the Scenery set (sets marked Soon can't be picked yet), the Disk limit, and whether to Include overlays; turn overlays off if you use simHeaven X-World or another overlay package. With streaming on, you can finish without selecting a region. When you click Finish, AutoOrtho downloads the tile index (a few megabytes) in the background; if that fails, it shows the error and the task in the task list, and you can turn streaming on later from the Scenery Library. Streaming can't be changed here while AutoOrtho or X-Plane is running.
  4. Image cache: one folder, its free space, and a disk cache limit (with a suggestion for that drive). The long-term cache and download folders are under More folders….
  5. Quality target: one zoom level everywhere, or an altitude profile (Airliner, General Aviation, Low VRAM). It shows what the target needs on this PC, can test your connection, and can suggest a target.
  6. Limits and ready: Use what's available (recommended) or your own limits, a last readiness check, and Start AutoOrtho when setup finishes (it waits if scenery is still being installed, or until streaming is set up).

Existing installations with valid paths and dependencies are detected automatically and are not forced through the wizard. The wizard remains available from the header overflow menu or Settings → Setup & Storage. If setup is interrupted, reopen the wizard from that menu; unaccepted wizard changes are discarded and the last applied configuration remains active.

docs.title: Application navigation
docs.text:
The application is organized around five primary destinations:

  • Home — what AutoOrtho is doing now (see Home below).
  • Scenery Library — scenery search, filters, installation, updates, package details, and scenery streaming (fly without installing regions).
  • Flight Plan & Map — SimBrief controls, loaded-flight details, and a map with two views: the Custom Map editor and the Cache view of what AutoOrtho has stored per tile.
  • Settings — Essentials first, every setting with Show all settings, search, exact numeric inputs, and Apply/Revert.
  • Diagnostics — health checks, searchable logs, export actions, and performance-report history.

The last destination and window geometry are restored on the next launch.

docs.title: Keyboard and accessibility
docs.text:
All primary workflows are keyboard accessible. Use Ctrl+1 through Ctrl+5 to open Home, Scenery Library, Flight Plan & Map, Settings, and Diagnostics. Use Ctrl+S to apply settings, Ctrl+Shift+R to revert pending settings, and F1 to open documentation. Statuses combine text, symbols, and color so they remain understandable without color perception.

AutoOrtho follows the operating system UI font and supports Qt display scaling, including 200% scaling. Search fields, tables, task actions, settings controls, and custom editors expose accessible names for assistive technologies.

docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Home answers four questions in order: is it working, are you getting the quality you asked for, what is AutoOrtho using, and do you need to do anything. What it shows follows the state:

  • Stopped: the status strip with Start streaming, Ready to fly (the checklist appears only when something is wrong), the quality target with the lights from the cost preview and an Edit link, the last flight, storage, and scenery.
  • Starting: mounting, waiting for X-Plane, and how much of the nearby scenery is already sharp while X-Plane loads.
  • Flying:
  • Scenery quality: % sharp at target over the last 30 seconds, the target, the time to sharp scenery after an area loads, and a ten-minute trend with blurry moments in red. Click it for the Auto-Tuning timeline.
  • Network, Computer and Graphics memory gauges: use against the capacity or your limit, coloured by headroom. The one auto-tuning finds is holding the scenery back gets a ◆ chip.
  • Activity: textures served, the share from cache, data downloaded, builds in progress, and how far ahead of the aircraft everything is already sharp (in minutes and nm). It also has a small radar of the tiles around the aircraft (green sharp, blue being read, amber below target, grey not loaded) with the prefetch corridor; click it for the map.
  • Auto-tuning: the last change and why, the number of changes and pinned values.
  • Paused: the same, dimmed, and the numbers stop.
  • After a flight: the last flight in full: the verdict, sharpness by phase, distance, duration, data and cache share, guard activations and what auto-tuning learned. Dismiss returns to the stopped view.

Notices (at most three, the most serious first) appear between the strip and the rest only when there is something to do: a target out of reach, auto-tuning advice, values kept from an older config, or a failed scenery install. Scenery installs show as a badge on Scenery library. Compact keeps only the strip, quality and gauges (and hides the navigation) for a second monitor. While streaming, the window title reads like Home's headline, for example AutoOrtho · 96 % sharp · 142 Mbit/s · Flying. With Minimize to the system tray when streaming starts, the window goes to a tray icon with the same text as its tooltip, and comes back when streaming stops.

docs.title: Essentials and all settings
docs.text:
Settings opens on Essentials: the quality target with what it needs on this PC, the limits, the folders and disk cache, the imagery source, seasons, night exclusion, SimBrief and whether the window hides while streaming. AutoOrtho sizes everything else for this PC. Show all settings (top right) shows every category; searching always looks through all of them, and opening a category from elsewhere in the app shows them too.

The four performance profiles are gone: the quality target (with its altitude profiles), the limits and the automatic sizing cover what they did. The minimum zoom level is now an Expert setting (All Settings), since the low-zoom base covers far scenery.

When an older config is converted and it set engine settings by hand, those values are kept, and Home says so: Review opens them in the Expert table, and Use automatic values puts AutoOrtho's own values back (press Apply to keep them).

docs.title: Applying and reverting settings
docs.text:
Configuration edits remain pending until Apply is selected. Revert restores the last applied values. If streaming is started or the application is closed with pending edits, AutoOrtho asks whether to apply or discard them. Settings that affect mount workers display a restart notice when applied during streaming.

Long-running operations appear in the persistent Activity panel. Completed and failed tasks remain available until dismissed. Only operations that can be stopped without corrupting files expose a Cancel action.

Use the header's Start Streaming action after readiness checks pass. The same action becomes Stop Streaming while AutoOrtho is running. Start and stop progress remains visible as an Activity task, and the application waits for mounts to stop cleanly before it exits.

docs.title: Scenery install path
docs.text:
This is the location that scenery will be installed to. Previously this defaulted to a user's existing X-Plane Custom Scenery directory, but that is no longer the case.

It should be possible to set this to a convenient location with enough room to install scenery packages. Each scenery package can take around 20-30GB.

This can be an external NAS or separate drive, but I have not tried all drive combinations. Speed of external storage will naturally impact performance to a certain degree. Plan accordingly.

docs.title: X-Plane install path
docs.text:
This is the X-Plane install location. Under this directory should be X-Plane's Custom Scenery directory. IT IS IMPORTANT THIS IS THE CORRECT LOCATION

From this directory AutoOrtho will create mount points and run the program.

IF THIS IS NOT CORRECT THINGS WILL NOT WORK RIGHT

docs.title: Download directory
docs.text:
This is the path that will be used to temporarily store zip files and other fetched files for scenery setup. By default this will be in under the user's home dir under .autoortho-data/downloads

For Windows users, it is highly recommended to set a Windows Defender exception to this directory otherwise expect VERY slow setup of scenery.

This folder can be set to any convenient location with enough space for scenery downloads (20-30GB per).

docs.title: User config file location
docs.text: The configuration file .autoortho is located in the user's home directory.

docs.title: Only changed settings are stored
docs.text:
The file keeps every setting with its comment, but only the settings you changed are active lines. Every other setting is written as a commented default:

# Maximum zoom level to allow. ...
# max_zoom = 16
fallback_timeout = 45.0

Here max_zoom follows AutoOrtho's default, so it picks up any future change to that default, while fallback_timeout keeps your own value. To override a default by hand, delete the # and change the value. A line you write yourself stays active even when it equals the default, until you change it in the app.

The file is written as UTF-8. Older files written in another encoding are still read, and the first save converts them: values equal to the defaults become commented lines, and retired settings (live_aopipeline_min_chunk_ratio, ephemeral_dds_cache_mb, max_concurrent_downloads, http2_max_connections, and the old waits maxwait, suspend_maxwait, tile_time_budget and use_time_budget) are removed after their values are migrated. The old waits have nothing to migrate to: the wait bands replaced them (see the Performance Tuning Guide).

docs.title: All Settings (Expert)
docs.text: Settings → All Settings (Expert) lists every setting with its value, its default and whether you changed it. Search by name or description, filter by group (Essential, Tuning, Expert), or show only changed settings. Double-click a value to edit it, or select rows and choose Reset Selected to Default. Settings that already have a control on another settings page are shown greyed and are changed there. Edits are applied with Apply and discarded with Revert, like any other setting. The Source column shows This PC for values scaled to your computer (below); Reset returns a setting to that value.

docs.title: Defaults scaled to this PC
docs.text:
A few defaults suit a mid-range PC but are wrong at either end, so AutoOrtho scales them to your cores and RAM when you have not set them yourself:

Setting Rule 8 GB, 4 cores 16 GB, 8 cores 32 GB, 12 cores cache_mem_limit a quarter of RAM, 2 to 8 GB 2 4 8 predictive_dds_memory_mb by RAM, 256 to 1024 256 512 768 live_builder_concurrency one per physical core, 4 to 12 4 8 12 background_builder_workers one per three cores beyond two, 1 to 4 1 2 3

These values are not written to the config file, which shows them as # (set for this PC; the packaged default is 4), so the file still suits another PC. A value you set yourself always wins. Set [tuning] hardware_baseline = False to use the packaged defaults instead.

After a connection test, AutoOrtho also starts each flight's download concurrency (provider_origin_initial_concurrency) at the number the test suggested, when the test measured the imagery source in use; the adaptive controller still moves from there. The Expert table shows that value as Measured. A download limit also caps how many downloads run at once (provider_origin_max_concurrency): about what the limit needs, with half again to spare.

docs.title: Resource limits
docs.text:
Settings → Limits sets what AutoOrtho may use of this PC. Each limit is Auto (worked out from the hardware) or your own ceiling:

Limit Auto What it holds back RAM (ram_gb) a quarter of RAM plus 0.5 GB, leaving X-Plane at least 4 GB or 20 % the memory cache and predictive build memory AutoOrtho picks; the low-memory brake engages when AutoOrtho goes over it Graphics memory (vram_gb) the card's memory minus xplane_vram_reserve_gb the budget the graphics memory guard checks the target against Download speed (bandwidth_mbps) no limit every download: the broker reads no faster than this, so other apps keep the rest CPU cores (cpu_cores) all physical cores but two (all but one on four cores or fewer) native texture-build threads, and the builder counts AutoOrtho picks Protect X-Plane's frame rate (protect_sim_fps) on in Auto mode, auto-tuning eases off background builds and prefetch when X-Plane's frames get clearly slower (see below)

Limits lower only the values AutoOrtho picks itself. A value you set by hand elsewhere is kept, and the guards warn when it is over a limit. The Expert table shows a lowered value as Your limits. Changing a limit while streaming takes effect at once: AutoOrtho resizes its memory cache, build workers, download rate and download concurrency without remounting. (Raising the CPU limit above what streaming started with takes full effect at the next start.)

Edits in the Expert table to settings a running mount can pick up (prefetch distance, live admission, background builders, memory budgets and the like) also apply at once; only the others ask for a restart.

docs.title: Connection test
docs.text: Test my connection on the Limits page (and in the setup wizard) downloads about 30 MB of real imagery from your imagery source, in rounds of 16 to 256 downloads at once, and reports the speed and the fewest downloads at once that reach 90 % of it. A typical run takes a few seconds. The result is kept in ~/.autoortho-data/connection.json; the download guard compares it with what the zoom target needs, and Suggest a target for this PC uses it. The test is disabled while streaming, because it would share the connection. Apple Maps and custom maps are tested with Bing, since they need a session.

docs.title: Guards: what your settings need from this PC
docs.text:
Under the zoom controls in Settings → Imagery, a panel shows what the zoom target needs on this PC, with a light for each resource:

  • Graphics memory: the photo textures X-Plane holds for the target, against the card's memory minus what X-Plane needs for itself ([guards] xplane_vram_reserve_gb, 5 GB), or against your graphics memory limit when you set one. Red when it does not fit, amber when close.
  • RAM: the memory cache plus about 1 GB for the app, against your RAM. Red when less than 6 GB is left for X-Plane, amber above 35 % of RAM or above the RAM limit.
  • Disk: free space on the cache drive against what the cache may still take (its limit minus what it holds now, plus the safety margin), and how much new imagery an hour of flying adds.
  • Download: the speed the target needs to keep up, against the last connection test and your download limit. Amber when it needs more than 80 % of the slower of the two.

Suggest a target for this PC fills in the sharpest fixed zoom level that both the graphics memory budget and the connection carry.

The estimate follows X-Plane's texture paging: full detail only near the aircraft, less further away, and textures stay loaded for about 20 minutes. It works out each flight phase (on the ground, departure, climb, cruise, or each altitude step in Dynamic mode) and shows the busiest one. For example, from cruise altitude ZL17 needs no more graphics memory than ZL16, because X-Plane never asks for the extra detail from that height. Treat the figures as estimates: wide screens, a wide field of view and turning flight hold more.

When a light is amber or red, Apply suggestion fills in the nearest setting that fits: one zoom level lower, a smaller memory or disk cache, or the automatic graphics memory or a higher download limit when your own limit is the only problem. Nothing changes until you press Apply. Guards never block anything. When the saved settings do not fit, Home's Readiness card lists PC resources with the reason. Set [guards] warnings = False to turn the panel and that check off.

Graphics memory is read from Windows' display driver information, from nvidia-smi or the AMD driver on Linux, and on Macs with Apple silicon is taken as about two thirds of RAM. When it cannot be read, the panel says so and does not warn.

docs.title: Low-disk brake
docs.text: When the cache drive has less free space than the safety margin ([scenery] storage_safety_margin_gb, at least 2 GB), AutoOrtho stops writing new cache entries until 1 GB more is free. Scenery keeps streaming; only caching pauses. Counted as disk_brake_activations. [guards] ram_brake = False turns this brake off too.

docs.title: Low-memory brake
docs.text: While the system has very little free RAM (below 1.5 GB or 8 % of RAM), or AutoOrtho uses more than its RAM limit, AutoOrtho pauses prefetch and background builds and holds its memory cache to half its limit. X-Plane's own requests are always served. The brake releases once free RAM has stayed above 2.5 GB (or 12 %), and AutoOrtho under 90 % of its limit, for 20 seconds. Each activation is logged and counted in the performance report (ram_brake_activations). Set [guards] ram_brake = False to turn it off.

docs.title: Starting values: the tuning plan
docs.text:
Before a flight, AutoOrtho picks starting values for the settings you have not set yourself ([tuning] hardware_baseline, on by default):

  • from the PC: memory cache, predictive build memory and builder counts (cores and RAM);
  • from the quality target and the connection: what the zoom target needs to keep up at its busiest flight phase (the same estimate as the Download line of the target cost panel), against the last connection test of this imagery source, capped by your download limit.
Setting Planned from Prefetch chunks per cycle Up to three times what the target needs per second, never more than the line carries (at least 64) Predictive build memory One texture of the target per background builder, within a quarter of the RAM limit (only raised) Parallel downloads ceiling What the line (or the download limit) carries, with the connection test's speed per download, and half again to spare Prefetch radius 30 nm scaled by how much room the line has over the need: 15 nm on a tight line, up to 60 nm with plenty Prefetch lookahead, prefetch lead time 10 min and 60 s with room to spare; up to twice (lead 2.5x) as long as the line gets tight, so prefetch starts earlier Wait for near imagery 1.5x the time one full near texture of the target takes on the line, 6 to 12 s (only raised) Wait while starting 1.2x the time to load a new area, 60 to 120 s (only raised)

Without a connection test only the first two are planned. Settings (Expert) shows these values with the source Target and line. Auto-tuning then fine-tunes from there in flight; a value you set yourself always wins.

docs.title: In flight
docs.text:
While streaming, AutoOrtho measures every 2 seconds how much of the nearby scenery X-Plane gets at the zoom you asked for (% sharp at target), along with download speed, errors, CPU, RAM and the flight phase. Every few seconds it looks at the last 30 seconds, works out what holds the sharpness back (the connection, the imagery server, the CPU, memory, too short a wait, or prefetch falling behind) and can move one setting one step. Settings → Auto-Tuning ([governor] mode, also on Essentials) picks what it does with that:

Mode What happens Auto (default) Changes the setting while streaming, checks the result (after 10 to 20 seconds, up to a minute when too few nearby reads or a change of flight phase leave nothing to compare), and undoes the change if sharpness or the bottleneck got worse by more than chance explains. Advise Works out the same changes but applies none. Home shows the latest suggestion with Apply, which uses it at once and keeps it for the next flights as a learned value (not a pinned one): auto-tuning may suggest moving it again, and Reset learned settings clears it. Off Uses the configured values. Sharpness is still measured.

It waits longer only on evidence. When a nearby read stops waiting, AutoOrtho times how long that imagery still took to arrive. The wait is raised only when most of it (80 % in flight, 90 % while a flight loads) arrived within the longest wait allowed, and never beyond what it needed. When most of it took longer, waiting would only hold X-Plane up, so the state is Imagery arrives late and prefetch looks further ahead instead.

It tunes prefetch only on evidence too. AutoOrtho remembers, per tile, what prefetch did for it: when it was queued, to which detail level, when its imagery was in, and whether it later left the memory cache. When X-Plane reads a nearby tile blurry in flight (not while a flight loads or after a jump), AutoOrtho records why:

What prefetch had done State What auto-tuning moves Never queued it, and the tile lay off to the side Prefetch corridor too narrow Prefetch radius Never queued it, though it lay ahead Prefetch corridor too short Prefetch lookahead Never queued it, while prefetch was paused Prefetch paused Nothing; Home names the pause (low memory, X-Plane's own downloads) when it keeps happening Never queued it, in a turn — Nothing (SimBrief routes cover planned turns) Queued only a coarser level than X-Plane wanted Prefetch asks for too little detail Prefetch lead time ([streaming] paging_lead_seconds, 30-180 s) Queued it, but it was not ready in time Prefetch starts too late Prefetch lead time, then prefetch chunks per cycle (not while the line is full) It was ready, then left memory Memory cache too small Memory cache (only while AutoOrtho uses under 80 % of its RAM limit) It was ready and in memory — Nothing (a failed download, for example)

A setting moves only with at least 10 such blurry tiles in the last 30 seconds and one cause behind at least half of them; the change is kept when that cause's share of nearby reads falls. When the scenery stays blurry with no clear cause, the state is Blurry, cause unclear: nothing moves, and after five minutes Home says so and points to the flight report.

The rules that keep it steady: one change at a time, a 30-second wait per setting (two minutes after an undo), bigger steps while a flight is loading and while the scenery is far below the target (under 85 % sharp), a two-minute settling time before a change that fixed a bottleneck can be eased back, and nothing above your limits. When live tiles queue for build slots (the DDS buffers and streaming builders) rather than for admission, auto-tuning raises Live builders (live_builder_concurrency) and resizes those pools while you fly, within your CPU-core limit and a quarter of your RAM limit for the buffers. Compute-bound means AutoOrtho's own processes use what your CPU-core limit allows them (or the whole PC is busy); X-Plane's CPU use alone does not count against AutoOrtho. A full download queue raises the downloads ceiling only when the adaptive limit has reached it; when the imagery server is setting the pace instead (Network-bound, server pacing downloads), prefetch narrows to give the nearby scenery what the server sends. Limits or settings you change while streaming reach auto-tuning at once: a value you set is pinned from then on, and new limits narrow the ranges it may use. Settings you set yourself are pinned and never moved. It never lowers your zoom target: when every setting it may move is at its limit for five minutes and sharpness stays under 95 %, it shortens prefetch one step at a time (listed like any other change, and eased back once the scenery is sharp again) and tells you what limits it (for example "the limit is your connection"), with links to the target and the limits.

Settings you set yourself, in Auto mode. A value you set by hand (now or in an older config file) pins that setting: the tuning plan and auto-tuning leave it as it is. While auto-tuning is on, Home lists the pinned settings AutoOrtho would otherwise manage, with Let AutoOrtho manage them (back to the automatic values, saved at once and taken over mid-flight) and Review (the Expert table, showing only your own values). Dismiss the notice to keep them; it comes back only when another setting gets pinned. Pinning a setting on the Auto-Tuning page counts as keeping it. There is no need to delete your config file.

The Auto-Tuning page lists the settings it may move, with the current value, the range your limits allow, where the value comes from (Baseline, Learned, Governor or Pinned), the last change and its reason, and a Pin button. A timeline shows sharpness, Mbit/s, CPU and RAM for the session; click a red marker to read that decision. Export tuning report writes the same as JSON to ~/.autoortho-data/governor/.

Protect X-Plane's frame rate ([limits] protect_sim_fps, on the Limits page): when X-Plane's frames take 20 % longer than the best 30-second average of this flight and it runs under 40 fps, Auto mode lowers background builders, lengthens the pause between background builds and shortens prefetch. Such a change is kept as long as the scenery stays at least 95 % sharp. The frame time comes from X-Plane's UDP data output, like the flight data; without it the option does nothing.

Smaller textures when graphics memory is short ([governor] allow_texture_cap, off by default, on the Auto-Tuning page). AutoOrtho estimates the graphics memory of the photo textures X-Plane holds: each texture at the finest detail X-Plane read in the last 20 minutes. The page's status line shows it against the graphics memory budget (your limit, or the card minus xplane_vram_reserve_gb). When it reaches 95 % of the budget and you allowed it, Auto mode builds textures above 4096 px (ZL17 on ZL16 scenery, ZL19 near airports) at 4096 px for the rest of the session: a quarter of the memory, with the detail of one zoom level lower. Your zoom target is not changed, and textures X-Plane already holds keep their size. Without the permission, Home tells you instead.

Learning across flights. In Auto mode, the settings that ended up away from their planned values are saved at unmount in ~/.autoortho-data/governor/learned.json, keyed by the zoom target, the imagery source and a salted hash of your local network, so the next flight with the same key starts there. Suggestions you applied in Advise mode are kept in the same file and used in Advise and Auto. Reset learned settings clears both.

Flight verdict. The performance report gains a Flight verdict section: Smooth flight, A few blurry moments or Often blurry, sharpness by phase (loading, taxi, departure and arrival, cruise), the number of changes kept and undone, peak download speed, brake activations, what was learned for next time, and a Tuning plan table: the target's need, your line, and for each planned setting the planned value beside where auto-tuning left it. Its Blurry moments by cause table gives, per phase, the share of blurry nearby tiles by what prefetch had done for them (the causes in the table above).

With [governor] record_samples = True (the default) each session's samples are written to ~/.autoortho-data/governor/samples-*.jsonl (counters only, no positions). Developers can replay them offline with governor.load_samples() and governor.replay() to check a change to the rules against real flights.

docs.title: Performance Tuning
docs.text:
AutoOrtho includes advanced performance settings that allow you to balance image quality against loading times and stuttering. These settings are available under Settings → Streaming.

Key settings include: - Wait for nearby imagery / Wait while a flight loads - How long X-Plane's reads of nearby textures wait for real imagery (the wait bands; distant textures never wait) - Fallback Level - How aggressively to find replacement imagery for failed chunks - Spatial Prefetching - Proactively download tiles ahead of your aircraft - Dynamic Zoom Levels - Automatically adjust imagery quality based on altitude

For detailed configuration options and recommended settings for different use cases, see the Performance Tuning Guide.

docs.title: Provider transport and working memory
docs.text:
The shared provider transport uses asynchronous HTTP/2 requests. Network and tile-build concurrency are bounded independently:

provider_max_in_flight = 320
provider_max_connections = 160
download_dispatch_workers = 4
provider_queue_timeout = 60
provider_adaptive_concurrency = True
provider_adaptive_controller_v2 = False
provider_origin_initial_concurrency = 128
provider_origin_min_concurrency = 64
provider_transport_trace = False
live_tile_admission = 16
tile_image_cache_mb = 96
cache_write_buffer_mb = 256
long_term_cache_write_buffer_mb = 128
native_partial_allow_incomplete = False
persist_partial_dds_cache = True
partial_cache_promote_startup_max_tiles = 0
  • provider_max_in_flight is the strict global pending-request limit. A reserved slice remains available for live X-Plane requests.
  • provider_max_connections bounds physical connections. HTTP/2 can multiplex multiple requests over each connection.
  • download_dispatch_workers applies completed responses; it does not limit network concurrency.
  • Adaptive concurrency raises a provider's limit after sustained successes and reduces it after overload responses or timeouts. Windowed v2 additionally requires utilized, backlogged windows before latency-based adjustments.
  • live_tile_admission bounds expensive concurrent tile construction while allowing JPEG retrieval to continue independently. Only reads that may build a detailed level take a slot: X-Plane's header chunk (read for every texture it loads) and reads of the base level skip it, so they are never stuck behind nearby reads that wait for imagery.
  • tile_image_cache_mb is a per-tile byte budget for temporary fallback RGBA images. Oversized ZL17 mipmap-zero images are compressed and released.
  • Cache-write byte budgets prevent slow storage from retaining an unbounded number of downloaded JPEGs.
  • native_partial_allow_incomplete trades strict row quality for shorter deadline stalls by using child-cropped lower-ZL imagery and missing_color.
  • persist_partial_dds_cache stores only exact, checksummed compressed rows asynchronously for faster repeat loads. DDM v5 binds each row's immutable source manifest to the bytes that were compressed.

docs.title: Bounded prefetch pipeline
docs.text:
prefetch_pipeline_v2 = True
prefetch_lookahead = 10
prefetch_max_chunks = 64
prefetch_admission_burst = 64
prefetch_radius_nm = 30
background_builder_workers = 2
predictive_dds_memory_mb = 512
persist_partial_dds_cache = True
prefetch_quality_mode = prefer_target
prefetch_quality_grace_sec = 5
strict_target_deadline_sec = 120
partial_cache_promote_startup_max_tiles = 0

prefetch_max_chunks bounds work published per producer cycle, while prefetch_admission_burst bounds one candidate's coordinator pass. Queue, candidate, tile, JPEG, and predictive-build limits are derived independently from provider and memory capacity. A lookahead of 0 permits unlimited route discovery, while retained candidates and admitted work remain bounded.

Quality modes are responsive (lower-resolution fallback after the normal wait), prefer_target (a short exact-quality grace period), and strict_target (no lower-ZL substitution in mipmap zero, with a hard deadline). Rows are sealed on their first X-Plane read. Late target-ZL arrivals can improve only a future cache generation, never the bytes or provenance already served.

docs.title: Performance Diagnostics
docs.text:
The Settings tab can create an end-of-flight performance report containing X-Plane DDS read latency, cache/network/build stage distributions, the slowest tile operations, and per-process memory/CPU timelines. Reports are written to ~/.autoortho-data/reports by default. See Flight Performance Reports for the metric reference and analysis workflow.

checkpoint_interval_seconds controls periodic atomic worker snapshots (10 seconds by default). If a worker is force-stopped, the report recovers its most recent stage histograms and gauges instead of retaining resource samples only.

For troubleshooting missing tiles or stuttering issues, see the FAQ.

docs.title: Native Pipeline Settings
docs.text: AutoOrtho includes a high-performance native pipeline that significantly improves DDS texture building speed. These settings control the native components.

docs.title: Native Pipeline Threads (native_pipeline_threads)
docs.text:
• Type: Integer
  • Default: 0 (auto-detect)
  • Config file: native_pipeline_threads = 0

Controls how many CPU threads the native pipeline uses for parallel operations (cache I/O, JPEG decoding, DDS compression).

Value Behavior 0 Auto-detect CPU cores, use all available (recommended) 1 Single-threaded mode (lowest CPU usage, slowest builds) 2-N Limit to N threads (balance performance vs other apps)

Recommendation: Leave at 0 unless you need to limit CPU usage for other applications.

docs.title: Persistent Predictive DDS Cache (persistent_dds_cache_mb)
docs.text:
• Type: Integer (megabytes)
  • Default: 0 (managed by the shared disk budget)
  • Config file: persistent_dds_cache_mb = 0

Size of the cross-session cache for compiled DDS textures. The deprecated ephemeral_dds_cache_mb key is accepted for compatibility but no longer creates a separate cache.

Set this to 0 to remove the cache's independent DDS-only cap and delegate retention to the shared file_cache_size budget. With disk-budget enforcement enabled, complete DDS files, DDM metadata, and partial-row sidecars all count toward the DDS percentage; JPEG source files receive the remaining percentage. If disk-budget enforcement is disabled, 0 is genuinely unlimited.

Value Behavior 0 Use the shared disk budget and DDS allocation percentage 1024-4096 Fixed, bounded compiled-texture cache 8192+ Larger fixed cache for repeat long-haul routes

Why disk-only caching?

AutoOrtho uses disk-only caching (no dedicated RAM cache) because: - SSD reads are fast enough: Reading a pre-built DDS from disk takes ~1-2ms, which is negligible compared to the ~100-500ms build time it saves - OS file cache handles hot files: Your operating system automatically keeps frequently accessed files in RAM - Simpler memory management: No need to configure RAM limits - the OS handles it naturally - Cross-session: Valid compiled textures eliminate repeat downloads and builds

Key properties: - Uses atomic DDS and metadata sidecar files - Validates provider/build metadata before reuse - Enforces the configured DDS and JPEG disk budgets - OS file cache keeps hot files in RAM automatically

Recommendation: Leave at 0 so the shared disk budget controls retention.

docs.title: Apple Maps Caveat
docs.text:
When using Apple Maps (APPLE) as your imagery source, downloads always use the Python HTTP client instead of the native libcurl client. This is because Apple Maps requires: - Dynamic authentication tokens - Token refresh on 403/410 errors - Special header handling

Other imagery sources (BI, EOX, ARC, NAIP, USGS, FIREFLY, YNDX, GO2) use the faster native HTTP client when available.

See the Performance Tuning Guide for detailed architecture information.

docs.title: Dynamic Zoom Levels
docs.text:
AutoOrtho can automatically adjust imagery zoom levels based on your altitude Above Ground Level (AGL). This provides: - Higher detail imagery when flying low - Lower detail (faster loading) imagery at high altitudes - Terrain-aware calculations — flying at 10,000ft MSL over 5,000ft mountains uses higher quality than 10,000ft over ocean

Configure quality steps in Settings → Imagery → Altitude-Based Quality.

See the Performance Tuning Guide for detailed configuration.

docs.title: SimBrief Integration
docs.text:
AutoOrtho can integrate with your SimBrief account to use your flight plan data for: - Dynamic Zoom: Use planned altitudes at waypoints instead of velocity predictions - Prefetching: Download tiles along your actual flight path, prioritized by time-to-encounter using SimBrief's calculated flight times

To set up SimBrief integration: 1. Go to Flight Plan & Map 2. Enter your SimBrief User ID 3. Click Fetch Flight Data after filing your flight plan 4. Enable the toggle to use flight data for calculations 5. Optionally adjust the Route Calculation Settings that appear below the toggle

docs.title: Route Calculation Settings
docs.text:
When flight data is loaded and the "Use Flight Data" toggle is enabled, additional settings become available:

Setting Description Route Consideration Radius How far (nm) to look for waypoints when calculating tile altitude. Larger values are more conservative. Route Deviation Threshold Maximum distance (nm) off-route before falling back to DataRef-based calculations. Route Prefetch Radius How far (nm) perpendicular to your route to prefetch tiles. The path is sampled uniformly along the route; this controls the width of coverage.

ℹ Real-time Changes: These settings take effect immediately when modified — no restart required. Use Apply to persist your values for future sessions.

docs.title: Storage safety
docs.text:
Settings → Scenery includes a configurable free-space safety margin. AutoOrtho shows cache usage and available space, estimates temporary and final package requirements, and blocks scenery installation when either destination is too small or not writable.

See the Performance Tuning Guide for detailed information and limitations.

docs.title: Approach
docs.text:
There does not appear to be a way to hook directly into the internal texture loading mechanism of X-Plane via plugins. Instead, this project acts as a virtual file system interface for orthophoto satellite imagery.

As needed, imagery is downloaded from the indicated satellite photo sources as areas are requested. Imagery files are detected by naming convention of {row}_{col}_{maptype}_{zoomlevel}.dds This is the standard convention for imagery created from Ortho4XP.

docs.title: How does X-Plane access scenery?
docs.text:
Let's look at how X-Plane accesses scenery. In the install directory of X-Plane there will be a Custom Scenery folder. Under this folder there will be a number of sub directories of scenery and a scenery_packs.ini configuration file. This is where X-Plane will look for scenery.

Under each scenery subdirectory, there will be an Earth Nav Data directory that contains a number of lat-lon named subdirectories. Under these subdirectories will be a number of DSF files that contain instructions for X-Plane for this set of coordinates.

These DSF files are picked up by X-Plane based on the area that you are flying. During flight initialization a set of these files around your takeoff location are loaded. While flying new DSF files will be loaded. This loading while flying happens asynchronously behind the scenes.

The DSF files can contain various instructions for X-Plane. What we are interested in for orthophotos are terrain files. The terrain files a DSF contains would then point to the textures requested for this terrain, including satellite photo textures. These files are typically .dds files, though that's not always the case.

DDS files can contain multiple copies of the same texture at reduced resolutions. These are referred to as 'mipmaps'. This allows X-Plane to just pull in the minimum amount of data that is required into memory at any given time. Typically the maximum resolution for a texture is only required while flying low and for close by tetxures.

docs.title: How this project leverages this setup (high level description)
docs.text:
This project effectively requires all the parts of normal orthophoto satellite imagery, except for the satellite photos themselves.

Existing mechanisms to create and manage DSF files, and related terrain files, still applies. X-Plane continues to reference these files as per normal.

This program will detect when DDS files are accessed and read from X-Plane. When X-Plane attempts to read a specific mipmap of a texture this program will pull down just the minimum required data and return this data to X-Plane. This happens behind the scenes and as far as X-Plane is concerned, it is continuing to read a normal filesystem.

Since we only download the minimum required data, this process is relatively efficient.

Data is cached in memory until a memory limit is reached, at which time older data will be purged.

docs.title: Warning
docs.text:
I highly recommend using the pre-packaged scenery packs provided with this tool.

However, it's entirely possible to use your own scenery, if you wish. This could be useful for situations where you want an area I haven't gotten to packaging yet, or want a different zoom level that what is provided.

This should be considered an experts-only feature though and assumes: * You are very comfortable with the command line * You are very experienced using Ortho4XP and with installing custom scenery * You are very familiar with filesystem concepts and managing your Operating System

If you don't have this experience, that's okay, but likely you will struggle adding your own custom created scenery. I would recommend that you familiarize yourself with each of these listed items before proceeding.

docs.title: Adding your own created sceneries
docs.text:
Ready to add your own sceneries? Great!

So as mentioned above, this tool effectively overrides the 'textures' directory that XPlane is pointing to in order to location satellite imagery that is referrenced by a scenery pack's terrain files.

Due to how XPlane identifies terrain information, these directories have been split up into reasonable sized pieces, which is why each provided scenery pack has numerous numbered directories.

This project creates a special pass through filesystem that mounts directories into a location that XPlane can find and intercepts requests to '.dds' files. This is handled through the magic of FUSE (Filesystem in UserSpacE). FUSE is a common and standard feature of Linux, but requires extra stuff for other Operatings Systems.s

Sceneries stripped of satellite imagery, likely still have coastline PNG files that must be preserved. These are simply passed through when requested.

You can take advantage of this setup for your own scenery that you have packaged: * Place your scenery directory in Custom Scenery/z_autoortho/scenery

When execute Autoortho will detect directories in that scenery dir and mount these in your configured Custom Scenery directory.

docs.title: Ortho4XP Usage Tips
docs.text:
Ortho4XP can generate scenery files without downloading photos, which is perfect for this project. In the config set skip_downloads to True

Since this starts with low resolution imagery until you get going, I recommend enabling high_zl_airports

So far I've been testing with a ZL of 16 for most tiles with increased ZL of 18 for airports. You may have want to play around with the ZL levels for best results.

Higher zoom levels will lead to increased resource usage and longer delays initially starting up flights.

docs.title: Build System
docs.text: AutoOrtho uses PyInstaller to create standalone executables for all platforms (Linux, Windows, macOS). PyInstaller bundles the Python interpreter and all dependencies into a single distributable package.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Install build dependencies:

pip install -r requirements.txt
pip install -r requirements-build.txt

docs.title: Building the Native Pipeline
docs.text: The native pipeline (aopipeline) requires additional dependencies and must be built separately for each platform.

docs.title: macOS (ARM64/x86_64)
docs.text:
Prerequisites:

brew install libomp jpeg-turbo curl

Build:

cd autoortho/aopipeline
make -f Makefile.macos
# Output: lib/macos/libaopipeline.dylib

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
Prerequisites:

# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt-get install libomp-dev libturbojpeg0-dev libcurl4-openssl-dev

# Fedora/RHEL
sudo dnf install libomp-devel turbojpeg-devel libcurl-devel

Build:

cd autoortho/aopipeline
make -f Makefile.linux
# Output: lib/linux/libaopipeline.so

docs.title: Windows (MinGW-w64)
docs.text:
Prerequisites: - MinGW-w64 toolchain - TurboJPEG library - libcurl for Windows

Build:

cd autoortho/aopipeline
make -f Makefile.mingw64
# Output: lib/windows/aopipeline.dll

docs.title: Native Pipeline Components
docs.text: Component Dependencies Purpose aocache.c OpenMP Parallel batch file I/O aodecode.c TurboJPEG, OpenMP Parallel JPEG decoding aodds.c ISPC texcomp, OpenMP DDS texture compression aohttp.c libcurl Native HTTP client

docs.title: Fallback Behavior
docs.text: If the native library is not available: - AutoOrtho automatically falls back to the Python implementation - All functionality works, just slower for CPU-intensive operations - Log messages indicate which path is used

docs.title: Building the Application
docs.text:
The Makefile provides targets for each platform:

# Linux (creates .tar.gz)
make lin_tar VERSION=1.0.0

# macOS (creates .app bundle and .zip)
make mac_app VERSION=1.0.0
make mac_zip VERSION=1.0.0

# Windows (creates installer .exe and .zip)
make win_exe VERSION=1.0.0
make win_zip VERSION=1.0.0

docs.title: Output Structure
docs.text:
PyInstaller creates a bundled application with the following structure:

  • Executable: The main binary (autoortho, autoortho.exe)
  • ao_files/ folder: Contains the Python runtime, compiled bytecode, and all dependencies

The ao_files folder is essential for the application to run. It replaces PyInstaller's default _internal folder with a more descriptive name.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
To run from source without building:

python -m autoortho

docs.title: Important: Do NOT delete the ao_files folder!
docs.text:
When you extract AutoOrtho (Windows zip or macOS app), you'll see a folder structure like this:

Windows (zip extraction):

autoortho_release/
├── autoortho.exe          ← Main executable
├── ao_files/              ← REQUIRED - Contains Python runtime and dependencies
│   ├── (many files...)
│   └── ...
└── ...

macOS (app bundle):

AutoOrtho.app/
└── Contents/
    ├── MacOS/
    │   ├── autoortho      ← Main executable
    │   └── ao_files/      ← REQUIRED - Contains Python runtime and dependencies
    └── ...

The ao_files folder contains the bundled Python interpreter and all required libraries. If you delete this folder, AutoOrtho will not work!

Common mistakes: - Moving only the .exe file to another location (without ao_files) - "Cleaning up" by deleting folders that look like temporary files - Anti-virus software quarantining files from this folder

If AutoOrtho suddenly stops working after it previously worked, check that the ao_files folder is intact and in the same directory as the executable.

docs.title: I see occasional blurry and/or green (missing color) tiles
docs.text: Missing color tiles (typically green) occur when AutoOrtho cannot retrieve imagery within the time it may wait. This section explains why this happens and how to minimize it.

docs.title: Why do missing color tiles happen?
docs.text:
1. Time Budget Exhaustion: Each tile request has a time limit. If chunks don't download in time, they may appear as missing color.
  2. Network Issues: Slow or unreliable internet connections cause downloads to timeout.
  3. Server Issues: The imagery servers may be slow or temporarily unavailable.
  4. CPU Limitations: If your CPU can't decode images fast enough, chunks may not complete in time.

docs.title: How to minimize missing color tiles
docs.text:
Option 1 - Lower Zoom Level (Most Effective): Each zoom level requires 4× more resources. Lowering your max zoom dramatically reduces missing tiles: 1. Open AutoOrtho Settings 2. Lower "Max Zoom Level" from ZL17/18 to ZL16 or ZL15 3. This reduces chunks per tile from 1024/4096 down to 256/64

Option 2 - Wait Longer for Nearby Imagery: 1. Open AutoOrtho Settings → Streaming 2. Raise "Wait for nearby imagery in flight" to 8-10 seconds 3. This gives nearby textures more time to download (or set Auto-tuning to Auto, which raises it when nearby imagery keeps arriving just too late)

Option 3 - Enable Full Fallbacks: 1. Set "Fallback Level" to "Full (Best Quality)" 2. Enable "Allow fallbacks to extend time budget" 3. This allows AutoOrtho to download lower-detail alternatives when high-detail fails

Recommended settings for minimal missing tiles:

maptype_override_zoom = 16
band_max_wait_seconds = 10.0
near_wait_seconds = 120.0
fallback_level = full
fallback_extends_budget = True

Trade-off Warning: Longer waits and extended fallbacks may cause longer loading times and occasional stuttering. See the Performance Tuning Guide for a detailed explanation of the quality vs. speed trade-off.

For ZL17, Allow incomplete native partial builds is an additional opt-in trade-off. Disabled (the default) preserves strict quality and uses the normal fallback path if any requested chunk misses its deadline. Enabled, it completes the row with cache/lower-ZL imagery and finally the configured missing color, so loading may finish sooner but X-Plane can retain a degraded patch for that flight.

docs.title: Why are there so many missing tiles even with "Full" fallback enabled?
docs.text:
If you're seeing many missing tiles with fallback_level = full, check these:

  1. Budget still limiting fallbacks: By default, even with "full" fallbacks, network fallbacks respect the time budget. Enable "Allow fallbacks to extend time budget" (fallback_extends_budget = True) to let fallbacks continue after the budget is exhausted.

  2. New area without cache: The first time you fly over an area, there's no cached data for fallbacks to use. Fly the same route again and you should see fewer missing tiles.

  3. All fallbacks failing: In rare cases (server issues, network problems), all fallback levels may fail. Check the AutoOrtho logs for error messages.

docs.title: How do I get the smoothest flying experience with minimal stutters?
docs.text:
Stuttering occurs when X-Plane waits for AutoOrtho to provide imagery. To minimize stutters:

  1. Keep the waits short: "Wait for nearby imagery in flight" at the 6-second default or lower
  2. Let auto-tuning help: Auto mode eases off background work when X-Plane's frame rate drops
  3. Use cache-only fallbacks: Set fallback_level = cache to avoid network delays during fallbacks
  4. Enable prefetching: Keep prefetch_enabled = True to download tiles ahead of your aircraft
  5. Increase prefetch lookahead: Set prefetch_lookahead = 30 or higher for faster aircraft

Recommended settings for stutter-free flying:

band_max_wait_seconds = 6.0
fallback_level = cache
fallback_extends_budget = False
prefetch_enabled = True
prefetch_lookahead = 30
# Keep the detail level you prefer; performance features apply through ZL17.

Trade-off: You may see occasional blurry or missing tiles, but your flight will be smoother.

docs.title: Why does loading take so long at startup?
docs.text:
At startup, X-Plane requests the initial scenery tiles. Loading time depends on:

  1. Zoom level (biggest factor): Each zoom level increase requires 4× more resources
  2. Number of tiles: More tiles = more total work
  3. Network speed: Slower connections = longer downloads
  4. CPU speed: Slower CPUs = longer decode/compress times
  5. Time budget: Higher budgets = more time spent per tile

To speed up startup without lowering detail: - Keep the shared HTTP/2 downloader and DSF-driven prefetch enabled - Use the 60-second tile-wide default unless you explicitly want longer waits - Keep the persistent compiled DDS cache enabled for repeat visits - Enable Persist partial DDS rows if you repeatedly load the same ZL17 areas; the first visit still downloads imagery, while later visits can reuse each validated row independently - Choose the fallback policy that matches your initial-quality requirement

Zoom Level Resource Scaling: | Zoom | Chunks/Tile | Relative Load Time | |------|-------------|-------------------| | ZL15 | 64 | 1× (baseline) | | ZL16 | 256 | 4× | | ZL17 | 1024 | 16× | | ZL18 | 4096 | 64× |

See the Performance Tuning Guide for detailed zoom level recommendations.

docs.title: What do the Performance Tuning settings mean?
docs.text:
Setting What it controls Wait for nearby imagery Seconds a read of a nearby texture may wait for real imagery (longer while a flight loads) Fallback Level How aggressively to find replacement imagery for failed chunks Fallback Extends Budget Whether to continue network fallbacks after budget is exhausted Prefetch Enabled Whether to download tiles ahead of your aircraft Prefetch Lookahead How many seconds of flight time to prefetch ahead

For detailed explanations, see the Performance Tuning Guide.

docs.title: What is the Native Pipeline and do I need it?
docs.text:
The native pipeline (aopipeline) is an optional high-performance component that dramatically speeds up DDS texture building (10-20x faster). It's written in C and uses true multi-threading via OpenMP.

Do you need it? - If it's available for your platform (included in releases), it's used automatically - If not available, AutoOrtho falls back to the Python implementation - All features work either way; native is just faster

Benefit: Significantly fewer stutters, especially during initial scenery load or when flying fast/low.

See the Native Pipeline Architecture for technical details.

docs.title: Why are Apple Maps downloads slower than other sources?
docs.text:
Apple Maps uses the shared HTTP/2 broker while retaining its specialized token handling:

  1. Dynamic authentication: Tokens must be fetched via DuckDuckGo proxy
  2. Token rotation: On 403/410 errors, the token must be refreshed
  3. Special headers: Requires Authorization: Bearer headers

Concurrent 403/410 responses share one token refresh, preventing refresh storms. Provider-side throttling can still make Apple slower than another source.

docs.title: I changed the settings but nothing seems different
docs.text:
1. Restart AutoOrtho: Some settings require a restart to take effect
  2. Clear cache: Old cached data may affect results. Try clearing the cache
  3. Fly a new route: Cached areas will use existing data. Try an area you haven't visited
  4. Check config file: Verify your ~/.autoortho file has the expected values

docs.title: What happened to maxwait and tile_time_budget?
docs.text:
They were replaced by one wait policy, the wait bands: how long a read waits depends on how near the texture is (see the Performance Tuning Guide).

Old setting Now maxwait (per chunk) band_max_wait_seconds in flight, near_wait_seconds while a flight loads tile_time_budget (per tile) the longest of those two waits use_time_budget always on suspend_maxwait always on: the first load gets ten times the tile budget

Old values in your config file are ignored and dropped the next time it is saved.

docs.title: Time exclusion re-activated after scenery reload
docs.text:
Symptom: You have "Default to Exclusion" enabled, the exclusion correctly deactivated when sim time showed daytime, but after triggering "Reload Scenery" the exclusion incorrectly re-activated and you see global scenery instead of orthos.

Solution: This issue has been fixed. AutoOrtho now preserves the exclusion decision made based on actual sim time during temporary disconnections (like scenery reload).

If you're still experiencing this issue: 1. Make sure you're running the latest version of AutoOrtho 2. If the state seems "stuck", restart AutoOrtho to reset to the default behavior

Technical details: When X-Plane reloads scenery, the UDP connection temporarily disconnects, making sim time unavailable. AutoOrtho now remembers the last decision made with real sim time and uses it during these brief disconnections, rather than falling back to the default_to_exclusion setting.

See Time Exclusion - Decision Preservation for more details.

docs.title: I see a messge in the logs, but otherwise things work fine.
docs.text: The log will log various things, typically info and warnings can be ignored unless other issues are seen.

docs.title: In XPlane I get an error like Failed to find resource '../textures/22304_34976_BI16.dds', referenced from file 'Custom Scenery/z_eur_11/terrain/'.
docs.text:
What's happening is that X-Plane has found a terrain file, but is not finding a linked texture. This could be caused by a few issues:

  • AutoOrtho isn't running
  • You may have broken the links from your texture directories to the AutoOrtho mount location. Perhaps you manually moved around directories after downloading these from the configuration utility.
  • The directory AutoOrtho is configured to run from is now different from the directory links the scenery packs point to.
  • On Windows 11 try uninstalling Dokan (and reboot) and install WinFSP instead. Or vice versa.

First verify that AutoOrtho is running and there are no obvious errors shown in a log. If it is running then verify that all the directory links are correct, and consider simply cleaning up and reinstalling scenery from scratch, keeping a consistent 'Custom Scenery' directory configured.

If in doubt, re-install the scenery packs.

docs.title: Something went wrong with scenery setup and I'd like to start again.  How do I reinstall?
docs.text: AutoOrtho checks for metadata for installed scenery packs in Custom Scenery/z_autoorth/**_info.json Where '**' is a shortname for each scenery pack installed. You can delete the corresponding .json file, and re-run the configuration utility and should be able to reinstall the scenery pack

docs.title: Do I have to download whole scenery regions?
docs.text: No. Turn on Stream scenery you haven't installed in the Scenery Library and AutoOrtho downloads each tile the first time X-Plane needs it. Installed regions are still used first, so you can install the areas you fly most and stream the rest. See Streaming scenery instead of installing regions.

docs.title: I use simHeaven. Should I include overlays when streaming?
docs.text: No. Untick Include overlays in the Stream scenery panel. simHeaven already provides roads, forests and buildings, and streaming AutoOrtho's overlays as well would duplicate them.

docs.title: Scenery streaming is on, but I see default X-Plane terrain in some places
docs.text:
Those tiles couldn't be downloaded when X-Plane asked for them, so X-Plane got them from its Global Scenery instead. Check that:

  • AutoOrtho was running before X-Plane started, and streaming was turned on before AutoOrtho started. Streaming changes take effect on the next start.
  • Your connection to GitHub works.

The log says which tiles fell back and why: look for not streamed yet; using Global Scenery and Tile stream: host returned ..., pausing fetches. The second means GitHub throttled downloads; AutoOrtho tries again after a pause. Reload the scenery or restart the flight once the tiles have downloaded.

docs.title: Why can't I change the Stream scenery settings?
docs.text: They're locked while AutoOrtho or X-Plane is running, because the streaming folders are mounted when AutoOrtho starts. Stop AutoOrtho, change the settings, and start it again.

docs.title: I installed scenery, clicked "Start Streaming," but X-Plane did not automatically start
docs.text: You have to start X-Plane separately from this tool. It's also best to start X-Plane after starting autoortho so that all new files and directories are picked up.

docs.title: IOError: [Errno 24] Too Many Open Files
docs.text:
On some Linux distributions they set the minimum open files limits. This is 1024. Since AutoOrtho is modifying and creating a large number of files at the same time, it can easily hit this limit.

To confirm Run the following command and see if the result is in the 4,096 at a minimum. 'ulimit -n'

While doing this you can also check the hard limit thats system wide. This should be in the 100,000s or millions in most cases. 'ulimit -Hn'

Fixing by setting a higher limit temporarily Open a new terminal window.

This command will set a filesystem max file limit just in case we are accidentally hitting that limit too... 'sudo sysctl -w fs.inotify.max_user_watches=100000'

Now we will set our user/process limit to something more workable with generating ortho dynamically... 'ulimit -S -n 8192'

When you check your 'ulimit -n' you should now see it at 8k (8192). Now, in the same terminal window, we can launch our autoortho binary: './autoortho_lin_1.4.2.bin'

Note: when you close your terminal window that you entered these commands into (or start another) it will no longer have this raised limit. This is a python safeguard, not a flaw. It helps protect you against scenarios where touching a large number of files can indicate issues (e.g. resource exhaustion, ransomware attacks, bad code, etc).

docs.title: On Linux this does not start/gives a FUSE error
docs.text: Make sure that your /etc/fuse.conf files is set to user_allow_other. You may need to uncomment a line.

docs.title: WARNING - FallbackResolver: Could not import AoImage for disk cache fallback
docs.text:
This can happen when the prebuilt AoImage shared library provided in the installation package is incompatible with your Linux distribution. The most likely incompatibility is the C runtime library and the easiest fix is to install autoortho from source and rebuild the AoImage library on your system.

You'll need to install basic tools like a C compiler and make. On Debian-based systems, this may be something like:

sudo apt install build-essential make

On Arch/CachyOS:

sudo pacman -S --needed base-devel

Then:

git clone https://github.com/ProgrammingDinosaur/autoortho4xplane.git
cd autoortho4xplane
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
make aopipeline

Quick sanity check:

python -c "from autoortho.aoimage import AoImage; print('OK')"

Suggested start script:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
ulimit -n 524288
cd your_autoortho4xplane_directory
source .venv/bin/activate
PYTHONPATH=/your_autoortho4xplane_directory/autoortho python -m autoortho &

Thanks to "clumsynick" for this fix!

docs.title: The program crashed and now I get an error when AutoOrtho attempts to mount
docs.text: You can clear mounts manually with the command sudo umount -f AutoOrtho. You may need to run this for each remaining mount. The mount command will list your current mount points.

docs.title: When using Windows I see an error using the run.bat file such as note: This error originates from a subprocess, and is likely not a problem with pip. error: legacy-install-failure
docs.text: This is likely due to having a very new version of Python and a package dependency that does not have a pre-built 'wheel' binary. Further in that error you will see a link to visual studio build tools that can be installed. You could also try downgrading your version of Python. For instance try uninstalling Python 3.11 and install Python 3.10.

docs.title: Downloading and extracting files takes a very long time on Windows
docs.text:
This may be due to Windows Defender real time scanning be enabled. You can temporarily disable this, which should make a difference, but it will be re-enabled automatically.

You can exclude directories, such as `C:\Users.autoortho-data' or wherever else you installed your download and cache directories.

docs.title: On Windows the executable/zip is detected as a malware/virus by Windows Defender
docs.text: That is a false positive. Unfortunately, Windows is very dev and opensource unfriendly. You can choose to ignore this false positive or not, it's your computer. Alternatively, you can run this directly via source.

docs.title: I get an error when running with scenery installed on a non-local drive or non-NTFS formatted drive when using Windows
docs.text: This is not supported. Use a local NTFS formatted drive.

docs.title: Flight crashes during loading, X-Plane logs show no detailed errors.
docs.text: AutoOrtho Tile Setup and imagery download can take up lots of time while loading the flight and X-Plane freezes in the meantime. MacOS doesn't like the app being frozen and if you click on it or change apps often the system might force close it. Crashing the Simulator. Disabling multithreaded FUSE helps in these cases. Solution: 1. Set FUSE Multithreading to disabled in the settings. 2. Retry loading and stay on the loading screen (be patient)

docs.title: I have an issue that is not here.
docs.text:
Please check the issues page of the repository. Before submitting an issue please search for already existing issues for yopur problem, as it may be duplicated. If your issue has not been reported please open a new one and include as much information as possible, for example: - Screenshots - Logs - OS - Version of AO and X-Plane you are using

With more information the debugging process will be easier.

After the issue is opened I'll gladly check it out as soon as my time allows. Keep in mind that this is a side project for me, so support might not be immediate.

docs.title: I have an issue with some part of the mesh offered in the scenery packages
docs.text: Currently this fork still uses kubilus1 base mesh, as such support is not offered for it right now, this will change with the new custom mesh. For now refer to the issues page of the kubilus scenery to see if your issue has been reported and hopefully a community fix has been shared.

docs.title: What is the objective of this fork?
docs.text: As the AutoOrtho Continued name suggests the main idea of this fork is to continue building upon kubilus1's codebase and to add more features while keeping the program updated with latest technologies, and offer active support to issues that may arise.

docs.title: What has been changed?
docs.text: This fork currently adds a revamped new UI, more autoortho options such as overriding max zoom, and quality of life features such as new imagery servers and download retries. For more detailed information of the changes of every release please refer to the releases page as detailed changelongs of every release are detailed there.

docs.title: What's next?
docs.text:
While the scope of this fork may change over time and soem features might never see the light of day the main things in development right now are: - MacOs Support - Completely rebuild the Base Mesh packages with newer Otho4XP versions to have newest mesh info and take advantage of new XP12 technologies such as 3D water.

Things in backlog that are planned be implemented later on (order does not matter): - Predictive Tile caching with Simbrief integration: Have the program monitor your flight or via simbrief flightplan infer where you are heading to and start caching imagery from further tiles to speed up loading times and decrease stutters when you reach a new area. - Tile caching monitoring: See what tiles have been loaded and cached by the software. - Merge hotbso changes to this fork to support seasons with AutoOrtho

docs.title: When will those features be released?
docs.text: There is no ETA. And there is also no guarantee of this changes being released at all. Keep in mind this is a side project that is mostly fueled by my free time, autism and hyperfixation. So development times are not guaranteed and are subject to change.

docs.title: Can I contribute to help?
docs.text: Sure! This is a community open-source project after all, and the more contributions the better. You can create your own fork and open a PR into this repo with code you would want implemented! I will review it and hopefully merge it to keep this project growing.

docs.title: Want some idea that you want implemented but can't code it?
docs.text: You can still contribute! Open a discussion with your feature suggestion and maybe someone or me will look at it and implement it if we find it useful or interesting!

docs.title: macOS shutdown and native pipeline stability
docs.text: The shutdown report identifies a reproducible application shutdown defect, with possible additional macFUSE/kernel involvement. The changes in this checkout remove the unsafe shutdown sequence and add bounded failure handling. Local live-mount checks passed on macFUSE 5.0.6, as detailed below. Validation of the built app on the reported macOS 27/macFUSE 5.4.0 combination is still required before claiming the reboot-level failure is resolved.

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
The attached autoortho-ui-log.txt describes a different session from the one-mount report: six scenery mounts on an external T7 volume, Darwin 25.6.0, and a performance session dated October 19. Keep those environment details separate from the reported internal APFS/macOS 27/macFUSE 5.4.0 case.

In that log, streaming starts at 08:48:32 and stopping begins at 08:48:38. Africa's fuse_exit is followed by cleanup at 09:08:38, exactly 20 minutes later. South America also takes 20 minutes. Europe receives its poison probe at 09:28:39 and has not completed shutdown when logging ends around 11:08. The per-worker tile counts remain zero. This demonstrates that X-Plane, large tile populations, and flight-time network pressure are not prerequisites. Two mountpoint cleanup attempts also fail with Resource busy.

The supplied sample establishes that the main thread was blocked in lstat. It does not identify the pathname or prove which Python generator issued the call. The implementation nevertheless contained several independent ways to produce that state:

  1. The parent synchronously lstated a .poison file inside the mount.
  2. Its FUSE getattr callback stopped the FUSE request loop with fuse_exit.
  3. Mount polling used os.path.ismount, which itself calls lstat.
  4. Worker cleanup called lexists and rmdir before checking mount status.
  5. macOS readiness detection resolved the mount pathname and invoked mount, both of which can block against an unresponsive filesystem.

The attachment does not contain the separate row_offset traceback, manager EOFError, or native oversubscription messages. Those were assessed from the written report and the corresponding source code.

docs.title: Changes by priority
docs.text:
Priority Problem Change P0 FUSE stops serving before macOS has detached it macOS shutdown no longer probes .poison or calls fuse_exit from that callback. The OS unmounts while the worker continues serving requests. P0 Parent or worker blocks while inspecting its mount Darwin detection uses getfsstat64(MNT_NOWAIT) and a private buffer. Path normalization resolves only parent aliases, never the mount leaf. Worker cleanup is deferred to the parent until detach and worker exit. P0 diskutil/umount timeout handling can still wait forever A dedicated /sbin/umount helper gets a deadline. Timeout signals the helper without an unbounded post-kill wait. A blocked helper is retained and prevents repeated helpers against the same path. P0 Shutdown claims success after losing ownership of stuck workers Surviving worker handles are retained. Failed detach keeps the workers, broker, stats manager, and logging available; startup refuses to overwrite that unresolved session. P1 One mount prevents all others from stopping macOS mounts detach concurrently, with bounded helper waits, rather than accumulating minutes per region. P1 Long texture/download waits prevent timely unmount The parent sends a one-time quiesce command over a private inherited pipe. Workers cancel queued work and wake native admission waiters without exiting the FUSE loop. This works with GUI standard streams disabled. P1 Lost stats manager raises into worker threads Stats reads/writes/mapping operations fall back to local counters on EOF or broken connections. Missing shared flight state disables speculative work. Rebinding preserves existing imported STATS references. P1 Native budgets sum to more than CPU capacity Thread reservations enforce a total per-worker limit. CPU capacity is divided across launched scenery workers, with a minimum of one thread each. Explicit per-build settings are capped. P1 Partial builds/cache reads bypass native accounting Cache batch reads use reserved thread counts. Partial builds reserve their full OpenMP default because their native ABI has no thread-count argument. Worker environment limits are set before native libraries load. P1 OpenMP workers spin while idle Workers default to OMP_WAIT_POLICY=PASSIVE and KMP_BLOCKTIME=0. User-specified wait policies remain supported. P1 Periodic threads continue after shutdown Tile cleaners have a wakeable stop event and are joined before tile state is cleared. Worker reload polling stops on quiescence. Stats batchers join their background thread after flushing. P1 A read crossing an already-served row returns missing-color pixels for the next row Found during live DDS testing. Partial commits now atomically preserve sealed rows while installing new rows; only installed rows are queued for persistence. Both native and Python partial builders have regression coverage. P2 row_offset NameError in partial mipmap success path The current source already uses startrow * bytes_per_chunk_row instead of that undefined variable. Regression coverage now includes the first, intermediate, multiple, and last rows, checking actual DDS byte offsets. P2 .app metadata reports 1.0.0 Bundle version fields derive from release VERNAME, or the project version for local builds.

The old native allocator divided CPUs by the number of active builds without changing reservations already in flight. On 12 cores, four builds could receive 12 + 6 + 4 + 3 = 25 threads. New admissions reserve remaining capacity under a condition variable and release it even when a build raises. Across six mounts on 12 cores, each worker gets a two-thread share.
