If mounts outnumber cores, each worker still needs one thread; that minimum can exceed the machine total. The budget concerns native compute, not the total number of sleeping I/O, network, and UI threads.

Admission is FIFO so a partial build needing its full reservation cannot be starved by a stream of smaller builds. Static sharing favors predictable CPU use; it can leave capacity unused when only one of several mounted regions is active. Measure DDS latency and throughput during the release validation rather than assuming a performance improvement from lower thread counts alone.

docs.title: Native warnings and limits
docs.text:
The worker is already launched as a fresh executable, and the FUSE options already specify foreground=True. Regression coverage preserves that setting. The warning about forking a threaded process does not, by itself, establish that Python multiprocessing forked the worker. A native FUSE library may launch mount helpers internally. Do not suppress this warning or attribute it to a specific component without the full worker log and native stack.

The original report's processes remaining in U/?E after SIGKILL are a kernel or filesystem-driver state, beyond what Python cancellation can repair. An absent mount-table entry is not sufficient proof of recovery. In particular, do not document worker SIGKILL as a reliable recovery procedure. These changes aim to avoid creating the bad shutdown state and to report failure honestly; they cannot recover an already wedged macFUSE kernel session.

While running tests locally, loading the installed /usr/local/lib/libfuse.2.dylib without mounting also caused CFRelease(NULL) in a process-exit destructor. That is separate evidence about this machine's native library environment, not proof of the reported macFUSE kernel failure. Callback unit tests use a stub driver. The subsequent live checks exercised the normal source worker entrypoint, which exits without running that native destructor.

docs.title: Live local check — October 31, 2026
docs.text:
Environment: macOS 26.7.1, Apple Silicon, 10 logical CPUs, Python 3.14.6, macFUSE 5.0.6, /usr/local/lib/libfuse.2.dylib. The test used temporary backing directories and actual macFUSE mounts, production worker supervision, shared statistics and download-broker services, and the production parent shutdown method. It reused mountpoints across cycles without launching X-Plane.

Scenario Successful cycles Total shutdown time One mount, verified file read 20 0.76–1.29 s Six mounts, verified file reads 3 1.17–1.24 s One mount, native partial DDS reads 3 1.18–1.40 s Six mounts, concurrent native partial DDS reads 3 0.96–1.16 s

The DDS input consisted of 341 cached JPEG chunks across ZL12–16. Reads checked the DDS header, 4096×4096 dimensions, and mipmap-zero rows 0, 1, 7, and 15. Identical source rows had identical compressed checksums. No network imagery was needed. Each successful cycle verified worker exit code zero, reaped PIDs, and disappearance of every test mount. The final independent process check found no test workers, brokers, managers, or mounts remaining. No force-kill or reboot was required for successful cycles, and no oversubscription messages or native partial exceptions were recorded.

The first DDS attempt exposed a real boundary defect: a 32 KiB kernel read at offset 507904 crosses the first 524288-byte data row, which begins after the 128-byte DDS header. Row zero was already sealed by an earlier read, so the combined row-zero/row-one commit was rejected and row one was served missing. The fix preserves row zero while committing row one. The subsequent DDS cycles passed, and regression tests reproduce the same read sequence for both native and Python builders. A harmless winreg import error logged on macOS was also corrected by restricting that import to Windows.

Detailed JSON results, logs, and the isolated test harness are saved locally under logs/macos-smoke-20261031/. These checks exercise source workers, cached imagery, and an older driver than the report. They do not cover a packaged-app bootloader, a 30-minute flight, or network stalls. The test used a three-second tile budget and disabled speculative prefetch during the DDS phase.

docs.title: Validation before release
docs.text:
Automated regression groups cover shutdown ordering, timed-out and busy helpers, retained worker handles, retry/restart guards, GUI-independent control pipes, cached mount-table reads, cleanup protection, manager disconnects, native CPU admission/cancellation, and exact partial DDS row placement. Run parent/UI tests separately from package-based texture tests: the existing suite mixes autoortho.py imports with namespace-package imports.

The expanded local verification passed 311 focused tests in two cleanly exiting runs: 247 texture/runtime/download/queue/cache tests and 64 mount/supervisor/UI lifecycle tests. Syntax checks passed for implementation/build files, and git diff --check passed. The Darwin mount-table ABI was checked against the local SDK (2,168 bytes), and the cached API returned the APFS root entry. The automated regression runs use stubbed mounts; the live checks above were run separately against the installed driver.

The broader Qt runtime suite aborted inside native QWizard code while opening the setup wizard during settings rendering. The selected asynchronous start/stop, worker-exit, and failed-close lifecycle tests passed. This is a remaining validation limitation; the full UI suite is not claimed as passing.

For local tests, load both applicable config modules in worker mode before starting pytest, then unset AO_RUN_MODE. This avoids rewriting the real user configuration during module import while allowing config-persistence tests to exercise writes to their temporary configuration files.

On a disposable test session or machine, validate the built .app with macFUSE 5.4.0 on Apple Silicon, and separately with FUSE-T if it is supported:

  1. Start and stop one mount without launching X-Plane. Repeat at least 20 times; every cycle must allow a new streaming session without rebooting.
  2. Repeat with all six regions. Record total detach time and worker exit time; a helper timeout must become a visible failure, never an indefinite UI wait or a successful stop while workers remain alive.
  3. Stop during cached reads, active downloads, partial native builds, and after a 30-minute flight. Verify cancellation, native CPU peaks, memory plateau, and the absence of continuing worker statistics after successful shutdown.
  4. Inject a manager disconnect and an unmount-helper timeout. Confirm that the application remains responsive, preserves ownership, and refuses restart until the unresolved session has actually stopped.
  5. Verify no worker processes remain after a successful stop, and verify both bundle version fields in the built Info.plist against the release version.

If a reboot-level failure persists with this sequence removed, collect the worker and parent stacks, loaded FUSE library path/version, and a macOS sysdiagnose for the driver maintainers. Avoid diagnostic commands against the stuck mount; the report already demonstrates that those commands can wedge too.

docs.title: Native crash diagnostics
docs.text: Mount workers collect crash evidence automatically on Windows, macOS and Linux. Start AutoOrtho and fly normally. The surviving application process records the worker's failure, so native faults do not need to reach a Python exception hook. All evidence stays in ~/.autoortho-data/crashes; nothing is uploaded.

docs.title: Native library rebuilds
docs.text:
The release workflows force a fresh pipeline build on Windows, macOS and Linux. AoCache, AoDecode and AoDDS are compiled together into aopipeline.dll, libaopipeline.dylib or libaopipeline.so. Third-party libraries remain build dependencies; this does not rebuild every bundled third-party library.

On macOS and Linux, release-bundle copies the compiler's output into the platform directory consumed by PyInstaller. The workflow records source and binary hashes in native-build.json and checks all three component versions against their source declarations. Packaging verifies the staged library and its source hashes for the target platform. A build failure stops the job.

Packagers may change Mach-O code signatures or ELF loader paths. The manifest describes the verified compiler output; POSIX crash reports also record hashes of the installed files after those transformations.

For a local macOS build, use make -B -C autoortho/aopipeline -f Makefile.macos release-bundle, then python autoortho/native_build.py record --platform macos --source-root . --directory autoortho/aopipeline/lib/macos --revision <commit>. Use Makefile.linux, --platform linux and lib/linux for Linux. The verify action checks hashes; versions checks the compiled component versions.

The vendored macOS static dependencies currently carry deployment targets newer than the Makefile's macOS 11 setting. A successful build on a recent Mac does not validate compatibility with older macOS versions; check those targets before publishing a release that claims older OS support.

docs.title: macOS and Linux
docs.text:
Before application or native-library imports, the worker enables CPython's C fault handler with a dedicated file descriptor that stays open until exit. On SIGSEGV, SIGABRT, SIGBUS, SIGILL or SIGFPE, it records Python thread stacks and requests the crashing thread's C stack with Python 3.14. C stack support depends on the OS and Python build; an unsupported build records that limitation in the fault log. Free-threaded Python can report only the current thread. This does not install Python callbacks for fatal signals, or change FUSE's existing termination and user-signal handling.

Each failed worker produces a bundle with a shared posix-<id> prefix:

  • .fault.log: fatal-signal traceback and supported C stack information.
  • .worker.json: PID, Python version, executable, native library paths and SHA-256 hashes, and existing core-dump settings. These are hashes of the actual installed libraries, including any packaging/code-signing transformations.
  • .images.json: loaded executable image paths and addresses, refreshed after the worker's runtime imports and before mounting FUSE.
  • .crash.json: parent-recorded exit code, signal, and whether shutdown had been requested. A native fatal signal during shutdown is still retained.
  • .system.json: outcome of OS crash-report collection, including why reports could not be obtained.
  • .complete: collection finished; the bundle is eligible for retention.

The parent collects OS reports in the background without delaying streaming cleanup. On macOS, it waits up to eight seconds for a readable .ips or .crash report with the worker's PID and a fresh modification time, and copies only that matching report. The native image list in that OS report can include libraries loaded after AutoOrtho's startup snapshot.

On Linux, it asks an existing /usr/bin/coredumpctl or /bin/coredumpctl for info matching the worker's PID, user, executable and a time window from startup through a short OS-reporting grace period after exit. It retries for up to eight seconds to allow the OS collector to finish. Output goes into .system.txt. Availability depends on systemd-coredump and journal permissions; this command does not export a full core image. Existing core limits and /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern are recorded without changing them.

This does not install a debugger, request administrator access, change global crash-report settings, or enable potentially large core files. Native faults still terminate with their original signal. SIGKILL cannot run a fault handler: the parent records it without claiming that a native stack or an OOM diagnosis is available. Normal exits and requested non-fatal stops discard their empty diagnostic files. The latest three completed POSIX bundles are retained when a new worker starts; active bundles and Windows reports are not pruned.

Crash files can contain private paths and process memory details. Share them privately with a maintainer. The POSIX crash diagnostics workflow checks real segmentation faults, aborts, normal exits and SIGKILL on Linux and macOS without FUSE or the simulator, and disables core files in its test children only.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text: Windows uses a separate bundled debugger process to capture native fast-fail, including a minidump and exception subcode. It also checks native DLL build provenance. See Windows native diagnostics for its build, packaging and evidence details.

docs.title: Performance Tuning Guide
docs.text: AutoOrtho includes advanced performance tuning options that allow you to balance image quality against loading times and in-flight stuttering. This guide explains each setting and provides recommendations for different use cases.

docs.title: Loading Architecture
docs.text:
AutoOrtho keeps the selected detail level, including ZL17, while reducing startup latency through:

  • one loopback-only HTTP/2 broker shared by all mounted regions;
  • bounded global request concurrency and per-request cancellation;
  • coalescing of identical imagery requests across workers;
  • DSF- and trajectory-driven prefetch only after X-Plane reports a valid flight connection;
  • a persistent compiled DDS cache for repeat routes; and
  • lazy regional download/build services so inactive regions remain lightweight.

If the optional HTTP/2 dependencies cannot start, AutoOrtho reports the error and falls back to the existing HTTP/1.1 request path.

docs.title: ZL17 partial loading
docs.text:
Mipmap-zero reads materialize and probe only the requested chunk rows. Sequential reads may schedule one low-priority row ahead after a pattern is established; live X-Plane work always takes priority. Partial rows use sparse compressed storage, so a one-row BC1 request uses about 1 MiB instead of allocating the entire 32 MiB mipmap buffer.

[autoortho]
# Strict quality remains the default.
native_partial_allow_incomplete = False
# Optional repeat-load cache for compressed partial rows.
persist_partial_dds_cache = True

Allow incomplete native partial builds finishes a row after its shared deadline with correctly cropped cache/lower-ZL imagery where available and missing_color elsewhere. This can shorten a cold load, but X-Plane may retain those degraded areas for the current flight. Leave it disabled for strict quality.

Persist partial DDS rows writes only exact, checksummed compressed rows through a bounded background queue. First-load behavior is unchanged; repeat visits can serve covered rows immediately and fetch only missing rows. DDM v5 stores an immutable source manifest for every row. Partial metadata never advertises mipmap zero as complete, corrupt records are ignored, and complete textures are promoted to the normal DDS cache. The row cache consumes additional space within the DDS disk budget. The Balanced, Quality, and Low Bandwidth presets enable row persistence; existing configurations retain the conservative disabled default.

docs.title: Download Concurrency
docs.text:
Broker-backed downloads are dispatched asynchronously: a single dispatcher thread owns the broker client socket and keeps many requests in flight at once. Downloader threads no longer block one-per-request, so real concurrency is set by the broker budget rather than by the size of the worker pool.

The broker queue wakes one idle coroutine per new request instead of waking all idle workers. Reprioritizing an existing item does not wake additional workers; cancellation hands off an unused wakeup so queued work is not stranded.

[autoortho]
# Maximum imagery requests in flight against the broker at any moment.
provider_max_in_flight = 320
# Upstream HTTP/2 connections the broker keeps open per provider host.
provider_max_connections = 160
# Threads used to settle completed downloads (coordination only).
download_dispatch_workers = 4
# Queue watchdog; HTTP timeouts begin only after the broker sends STARTED.
provider_queue_timeout = 60
Setting Default Range Notes provider_max_in_flight 320 8-1024 Strict cap. A reserved slice (25%) is held for live, X-Plane-visible tiles so prefetch and healing can never starve them. provider_max_connections 160 1-256 Effective value is min(provider_max_in_flight, provider_max_connections). This preserves throughput when a provider negotiates HTTP/1.1 rather than multiplexed HTTP/2. download_dispatch_workers 4 1-16 Small fixed pool that finalises completed requests; increasing it does not increase download concurrency. provider_queue_timeout 60 5-600 seconds Maximum broker/adaptive queue wait. It is separate from provider connect/read/pool timeouts.

For connection tuning, keep provider_max_in_flight near twice provider_max_connections. Compare 128, 160, and 200 connections with repeated cold-cache runs before choosing a value. Counts beyond the provider's throughput knee increase queueing, timeouts, and throttling without improving completed JPEGs per second.

docs.title: Strict admission
docs.text:
The dispatch stage never falls back to a synchronous HTTP request just because it is busy. When provider_max_in_flight is exhausted, work is parked in a bounded, priority-ordered deferred queue and admitted as soon as a slot frees up; live tiles jump ahead of queued prefetch work. If the deferred queue itself is full, the chunk is quietly requeued onto the normal work queue rather than downloaded inline, so the configured concurrency is a hard ceiling on real provider load.

Because downloader threads only coordinate (they no longer block on the network), the pool is sized by download_dispatch_workers whenever a broker is configured. fetch_threads still sizes the pool when no broker is available.

docs.title: Adaptive per-provider concurrency
docs.text:
The broker measures every upstream request, so it enforces an additional per-origin (scheme://host) limit on top of the global budget. The controller is AIMD:

  • Additive increase — after at least one full concurrency window of fast, successful responses (and never fewer than provider_origin_success_threshold) the limit grows by provider_origin_increase_step.
  • Multiplicative decrease — a 429, any 5xx, or a timeout/connection error multiplies the limit by provider_origin_decrease_factor (clamped at provider_origin_min_concurrency) and starts a cooldown of provider_origin_cooldown_seconds during which further failures do not compound the reduction.
  • 403 and 410 are treated as neutral: they are per-tile answers, not overload signals, so they neither raise nor lower the limit.
  • Slow successful responses do not raise the limit, and ramp-up pauses during the overload cooldown. This prevents the controller from oscillating back into saturation immediately after reducing concurrency.

Requests that cannot get an origin permit are parked in the broker's per-origin backlog and resumed in priority order, so a throttled origin never blocks another one and low-volume origins keep their own floor (provider_origin_min_concurrency).

After the first response identifies the negotiated protocol, HTTP/1.x origins are capped at provider_max_connections. This prevents hundreds of broker tasks from timing out while waiting for a smaller HTTP/1.1 connection pool. HTTP/2 origins may continue ramping toward provider_max_in_flight.

[autoortho]
# Adaptive per-origin concurrency (broker-side).
provider_adaptive_concurrency = True
# Use two-second throughput/latency/error windows instead of legacy AIMD.
provider_adaptive_controller_v2 = False
provider_origin_initial_concurrency = 128
provider_origin_min_concurrency = 64
provider_transport_trace = False
# 0 => use provider_max_in_flight as the per-origin ceiling.
provider_origin_max_concurrency = 0
provider_origin_increase_step = 1
provider_origin_success_threshold = 8
provider_origin_decrease_factor = 0.5
provider_origin_cooldown_seconds = 5.0
Setting Default Range Notes provider_adaptive_concurrency True bool Disable to use a fixed per-origin limit equal to the ceiling. provider_adaptive_controller_v2 False bool Uses windowed proportional probing and severity-based reductions. Low-demand windows hold, and latency needs consecutive utilized evidence. provider_origin_initial_concurrency 128 0-1024 Starting limit for each origin. provider_origin_min_concurrency 64 1-256 Floor for real overload reductions. Latency-only reductions also respect 50% of the last stable point. provider_transport_trace False bool Aggregates supported httpcore connection lifecycle counters without retaining URLs. provider_origin_max_concurrency 0 0-1024 0 means provider_max_in_flight. Always clamped to the global max_concurrency. provider_origin_increase_step 1 1-64 Permits added per successful ramp step. provider_origin_success_threshold 8 1-4096 Consecutive successes required before a ramp step. provider_origin_decrease_factor 0.5 0.1-0.95 Multiplier applied on overload. provider_origin_cooldown_seconds 5.0 0-60 Suppresses repeated cuts while a reduction settles.

The three most useful expert controls—initial concurrency, decrease factor, and cooldown—are available in Settings → Advanced → Engine, Network and Memory → Provider Download Transport → Advanced adaptive tuning. The section is collapsed by default to keep unsafe tuning away from normal users.

Current limits, active requests and throttle counts are exposed through the broker stats endpoint (HTTP2Broker.server_stats()) and, when profiling is enabled, as the broker.origin_limit.<origin> gauge plus broker.origin_limit_change stage records.

docs.title: Transport
docs.text: Broker replies are multipart: one MessagePack frame with the response metadata and a second frame carrying the raw JPEG bytes. The image body is therefore never copied into or out of a MessagePack buffer. Requests and control messages remain single-frame, and clients still accept a legacy embedded body for compatibility.

docs.title: Legacy settings
docs.text:
max_concurrent_downloads and http2_max_connections are migrated to provider_max_in_flight and provider_max_connections only when the modern key is absent from the user's file. A present modern key is always authoritative, even when its value equals the packaged default. Deprecated keys are normalized during the next save so migration messages do not recur.

fetch_threads still sizes the downloader thread pool, but those threads now only feed the asynchronous dispatch stage (and serve the direct HTTP/1.1 fallback path). It no longer caps how many downloads can be in flight.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
For most users, three things on Settings → Essentials are all the tuning needed:

Setting What it does Quality target The zoom level you want (fixed, or by altitude). The panel under it shows what it needs from this PC and can suggest a target that fits. Limits What AutoOrtho may use: RAM, graphics memory, download speed and CPU cores. Auto works them out from the hardware. Auto-tuning Auto adjusts the engine settings while you fly to reach the target within the limits; Advise only suggests changes. See Auto-tuning.

The sections below describe the engine settings themselves, for when you want to set one by hand (a value you set is kept and never moved by auto-tuning).

docs.title: Flight Performance Reports
docs.text:
AutoOrtho creates a profiling report for every mounted flight session. Profiling starts immediately before the first scenery worker launches and finishes after all scenery workers stop, so the report covers X-Plane-visible tile requests, background prefetch work, and shutdown.

Reports are written to:

~/.autoortho-data/reports/performance-<timestamp>-<session-id>/
├── report.md
├── report.json
└── process-<pid>-<role>.json

report.md is the human-readable starting point. report.json contains the complete one-second resource timeline, latency histograms, slow-operation records, final counters, relevant configuration, gauges, and individual process profiles.

The Diagnostics destination lists these reports newest-first and loads the selected report without blocking the application. Use Open Report for the full file or Open Folder to inspect the accompanying JSON and per-process profiles.

docs.title: What is measured
docs.text:
Stage What it identifies fuse.dds_read Total time from an X-Plane DDS read until bytes are returned fuse.tile_lock_wait Concurrent reads blocked behind work on the same tile tile.cache_lookup In-memory tile lookup/open overhead cache.dds_load Persistent compiled DDS disk read and decompression cache.jpeg_batch_read Source JPEG cache I/O chunk.queue_wait Time a download waits for a fetch worker network.http_request Map provider/network request latency tile.collect_chunks Cache collection plus waiting for missing chunks image.fallback_resolve Disk/mipmap fallback work for missing chunks image.compose Progressive image assembly and fallback processing dds.builder_pool_wait Wait for a streaming DDS builder dds.buffer_pool_wait Wait for a preallocated DDS output buffer dds.native_compute Native JPEG decode and DDS compression dds.python_compress Python-path DDS compression tile.mipmap_build Complete mipmap construction

Stage durations are inclusive. Nested stages overlap, so totals must not be added together. Start with fuse.dds_read, then use the nested stage with the largest p95/max latency to locate the bottleneck.

Every AutoOrtho process samples RSS, USS, virtual memory, CPU, thread count, and I/O once per second. On macOS, each worker also records physical footprint so compressed/swapped native memory is visible. The report ranks processes by peak physical footprint on macOS or RSS elsewhere, and shows retained RSS growth. Native decode/buffer pools, tile counts, open references, and queue depth are tracked as resource gauges. Long or sub-second sessions use peak-preserving adaptive downsampling, keeping report memory bounded while retaining spikes and full-session coverage.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The Settings → Logging & Reports → Performance Diagnostics section controls the normal profiling options:

[diagnostics]
performance_profiling = True
sample_interval_seconds = 1.0
slow_operation_ms = 250.0
max_slow_operations = 200
python_allocation_tracing = False
report_dir = ~/.autoortho-data/reports
max_reports = 20

Normal profiling uses bounded histograms and slow-operation heaps to avoid growing with the number of tile requests. python_allocation_tracing is different: it adds file-and-line Python allocation growth, but materially changes performance and cannot see native C image/DDS buffers. Enable it only for a dedicated memory diagnostic flight, then disable it before comparing normal latency.

docs.title: Reading a report
docs.text:
1. Check Diagnostic flags for queue saturation, network latency, pool contention, native build cost, or retained memory.
  2. In Memory by process, identify the worker with the largest peak and RSS growth. Correlate its peak with tile/cache/pool gauges and the raw timeline.
  3. In Slowest stages, compare p95 and max, not only averages. A low average with a very high p99 is a stutter source.
  4. In Slowest individual operations, follow repeated tile IDs and outcomes to distinguish a single bad provider response from systemic contention.
  5. Use report.json for plotting or comparing sessions after changing one tuning parameter.

docs.title: Zoom Level (Critical Performance Factor)
docs.text: The Max Zoom Level setting has the most significant impact on loading times and resource usage. Understanding this is crucial for optimizing performance.

docs.title: How Zoom Levels Work
docs.text:
Each zoom level doubles the resolution in both dimensions, meaning each zoom level increase requires 4× the resources of the previous level:

Zoom Level Chunks per Tile Relative Resources Typical Use ZL14 16 (4×4) 1× (baseline) Low detail, fast loading ZL15 64 (8×8) 4× Medium detail ZL16 256 (16×16) 16× High detail (default) ZL17 1024 (32×32) 64× Very high detail ZL18 4096 (64×64) 256× Maximum detail, slowest

docs.title: Impact on Performance
docs.text:
Downloads: At ZL17, you need to download 4× more image chunks than ZL16. At ZL18, that's 16× more than ZL16.

Processing: Each chunk must be decoded (JPEG→RGB) and compressed (RGB→DDS). More chunks = more CPU time.

Memory: Higher zoom levels require more RAM to hold all the image data during processing.

Storage: Cache size grows exponentially with zoom level.

docs.title: Recommendations by System
docs.text: System Type Recommended Max Zoom Notes Low-end / Slow internet ZL15 Fastest loading, acceptable quality Mid-range ZL16 Good balance (default) High-end / Fast internet ZL17 High quality, longer loading Enthusiast ZL18 Maximum quality, expect long loads

docs.title: Example: Loading Time Impact
docs.text:
Assuming 50ms average per chunk download:

Zoom Level Chunks Theoretical Min Time ZL15 64 ~3.2 seconds ZL16 256 ~12.8 seconds ZL17 1024 ~51.2 seconds ZL18 4096 ~3.4 minutes

Note: Actual times vary based on parallelism, caching, and network conditions. These are theoretical minimums to illustrate the exponential scaling.

docs.title: Config File Setting
docs.text:
# Maximum zoom level for imagery (14-18)
# Higher = better quality but exponentially longer loading times
# Each level increase = 4× more resources needed
maptype_override_zoom = 16

Tip: If you're experiencing long loading times or frequent missing tiles, consider lowering your max zoom level before adjusting other settings.

docs.title: Wait Policy (wait bands)
docs.text:
How long one of X-Plane's texture reads may wait for real imagery depends on how near the texture is. This is the only wait policy: it replaced the per-chunk maxwait, the tile time budget (tile_time_budget, use_time_budget) and the startup extension (suspend_maxwait), which old config files may still contain and which are now ignored.

Band Which reads Waits up to Near X-Plane wants mipmap 0 or 1: the texture is next to the camera band_max_wait_seconds in flight, near_wait_seconds while a flight starts Middle A reduced level the same as near Far The base level (one low-zoom chunk) far_wait_seconds: it gets the best data at hand, and the real data is fetched behind it

docs.title: Wait for Nearby Imagery in Flight (band_max_wait_seconds)
docs.text:
• Type: Float (seconds)
  • Default: 6
  • Config file: [streaming] band_max_wait_seconds = 6.0
  • UI: Settings → Streaming → "Wait for nearby imagery in flight"

Longer waits give sharper nearby scenery on a slow connection, but X-Plane may pause longer on a texture. Each row of chunks may use what is left of the read's wait. Auto-tuning (Auto mode) raises it when nearby reads time out but the imagery arrives soon after.

docs.title: Wait While a Flight Loads (near_wait_seconds)
docs.text:
• Type: Float (seconds)
  • Default: 60
  • Config file: [streaming] near_wait_seconds = 60.0
  • UI: Settings → Streaming → "Wait while a flight loads"

While a flight starts (the loading screen and the time parked after it) and after a jump to another place, X-Plane does not read those textures again for a while, so nearby reads may wait much longer.

docs.title: Tile budget
docs.text:
A tile's budget across all its reads is the longest of the two waits above (60 s by default), so no band's wait is cut short. The budget only advances while X-Plane is reading the tile; time spent on other tiles between reads does not count. When it runs out, the tile is built with whatever has arrived and any incomplete areas use the fallbacks below, then missing_color. Before X-Plane first connects (the first loading screen), a tile may take ten times as long, at most 30 minutes.

Both waits apply at once while streaming.

docs.title: Fallback System
docs.text: When chunks fail to download in time, the fallback system provides alternative imagery to prevent missing tiles.

docs.title: Fallback Level (fallback_level)
docs.text:
• Type: String (none, cache, full)
  • Default: cache
  • Config file: fallback_level = cache

Controls which fallback mechanisms are enabled:

Level Fallback 1 (Disk Cache) Fallback 2 (Scale Mipmaps) Fallback 3 (Network) Use Case none ❌ Disabled ❌ Disabled ❌ Disabled Fastest, may have green/missing tiles cache ✅ Enabled ✅ Enabled ❌ Disabled Balanced - uses cached data only full ✅ Enabled ✅ Enabled ✅ Enabled Best quality - can download lower-detail alternatives

Fallback Chain Explained:

  1. Fallback 1 - Disk Cache: Searches your local cache for a lower-zoom version of the same imagery. Fast and free.

  2. Fallback 2 - Scale from Mipmaps: Scales imagery from already-built lower-detail mipmap levels. Very fast.

  3. Fallback 3 - Network Download: Downloads lower-detail imagery on-demand from the server. Slowest but provides the best fill-in quality.

Recommendation: Use cache for most users. Use full if you have fast internet and prefer complete imagery over speed.

docs.title: Fallback Extends Budget (fallback_extends_budget)
docs.text:
• Type: Boolean (True/False)
  • Default: False
  • Config file: fallback_extends_budget = False

Only applies when fallback_level = full.

When enabled, network fallbacks (Fallback 3) will continue even after the tile time budget is exhausted. This prioritizes image quality over strict timing.

Setting Behavior Effect False (default) Fallbacks respect budget Faster loading, may have some missing tiles True Fallbacks ignore budget Better quality, may cause longer load times

When to enable: - You prioritize having complete imagery over loading speed - You have a fast, reliable internet connection - You don't mind occasional longer loading times

When to keep disabled: - You want predictable, stutter-free performance - Your internet is slow or unreliable - Loading speed is more important than perfect imagery

docs.title: Extended Fallback Timeout (fallback_timeout)
docs.text:
• Type: Float (seconds)
  • Default: 30
  • Range: 10 - 120 seconds
  • Config file: fallback_timeout = 30

Only applies when fallback_extends_budget = True.

When extended fallbacks are enabled, this is one shared extension for the entire tile. Multiple block reads and fallback levels cannot restart it.

Value Total Extra Time Use Case 10s Up to 10 seconds Fast - minimize extra wait 30s Up to 30 seconds Balanced default 60s Up to 60 seconds Quality on slower providers 120s Up to 120 seconds Explicit maximum-quality choice

Example calculation: - tile budget = 60 s (the longest wait, see Wait Policy) - fallback_timeout = 30s - Total worst-case tile time: 60s + 30s = 90 seconds

Recommendation: Start with 30 seconds. Increase it only when complete initial imagery is more important than a predictable loading deadline.

docs.title: Startup Loading Behavior
docs.text:
While a flight starts, nearby reads wait up to near_wait_seconds (see Wait Policy). Before X-Plane has ever sent flight data (the first "Reading new scenery files" screen), a tile's budget is ten times the normal one. Temporary disconnects (for example from stuttering) do not bring the longer budget back.

Stall Detection: AutoOrtho monitors download progress and will log warnings if downloads appear stalled: - After 60 seconds with no successful downloads: "Downloads appear slow..." warning - After 180 seconds with no successful downloads: "⚠️ DOWNLOADS STALLED..." warning

These warnings help identify server-side throttling vs client-side issues.

Note: If you experience very long loading times (>5 minutes stuck at "Reading scenery files"), this may indicate: - Server throttling (especially with BI/Bing imagery during high-traffic periods) - Network connectivity issues - Very high zoom level with slow internet connection

Troubleshooting Long Loading Times: 1. Check AutoOrtho logs for "Downloads appear slow" or "DOWNLOADS STALLED" warnings - these indicate server throttling 2. Try a different imagery source (GO2, EOX) to rule out server-specific issues 3. Lower your max zoom level temporarily to reduce download volume 4. Ensure your file cache is enabled - subsequent flights load much faster 5. If issues persist, lower Wait while a flight loads (near_wait_seconds) for faster loads (may result in more blurry tiles initially)

docs.title: Dynamic Zoom Levels
docs.text: The Dynamic Zoom system automatically adjusts imagery quality based on your altitude Above Ground Level (AGL). This provides higher detail when flying low and saves resources at high altitudes where detail matters less.

docs.title: Why AGL Instead of MSL?
docs.text:
AutoOrtho uses AGL (Above Ground Level) altitude from X-Plane's y_agl dataref rather than MSL (Mean Sea Level) pressure altitude. This provides more accurate terrain-aware imagery quality:

Scenario MSL Altitude Terrain Elevation AGL Altitude Zoom Decision Flying over ocean 10,000ft 0ft 10,000ft AGL Lower zoom OK Flying over mountains 10,000ft 5,000ft 5,000ft AGL Higher zoom needed Approaching mountain airport 8,000ft 7,000ft 1,000ft AGL Maximum zoom

With AGL, you automatically get higher quality imagery when flying low over terrain, regardless of the terrain's MSL elevation.

docs.title: Enable Dynamic Zoom (max_zoom_mode)
docs.text:
• Type: String (fixed, dynamic)
  • Default: fixed
  • Config file: max_zoom_mode = fixed
Mode Description fixed Use the same zoom level everywhere (traditional behavior) dynamic Automatically adjust zoom based on AGL altitude

docs.title: Configuring Quality Steps
docs.text:
Quality Steps define zoom levels for different altitude ranges. Each step specifies: - Altitude (AGL): The altitude threshold in feet above ground - Zoom Level: The maximum zoom level for normal tiles - Airports Zoom Level: The maximum zoom level near airports (can be higher for detail)

The inline editor under Settings → Imagery → Altitude-Based Quality shows the resulting altitude ranges and preview chart, includes Airliner/General Aviation/Low VRAM presets, and supports undo, redo, reset, and keyboard row removal. Changes remain transactional until Apply is selected.

Example configuration:

Altitude (AGL) Normal ZL Airports ZL Use Case 0ft+ ZL17 ZL18 On ground / very low 5,000ft+ ZL16 ZL17 Low altitude flight 15,000ft+ ZL15 ZL16 Medium altitude 30,000ft+ ZL14 ZL15 High altitude cruise

How altitude prediction works:

When a tile is requested, AutoOrtho predicts your altitude when you'll be closest to that tile:

  1. Gets your current position, heading, speed, and vertical speed
  2. Calculates when you'll be closest to the tile
  3. Predicts your AGL altitude at that time
  4. Selects the appropriate zoom level for that predicted altitude

This means tiles ahead of you during a descent will load at higher detail than tiles behind you.

docs.title: Fallback Behavior
docs.text: When X-Plane DataRefs are not available (before flight starts, loading screens): - Dynamic zoom falls back to the base step (0ft AGL quality level) - This ensures tiles load at maximum configured quality during scenery loading

docs.title: Spatial Prefetching
docs.text: The prefetching system proactively downloads tiles ahead of your aircraft to reduce in-flight stuttering.

docs.title: Enable Prefetching (prefetch_enabled)
docs.text:
• Type: Boolean (True/False)
  • Default: True
  • Config file: prefetch_enabled = True

When enabled, AutoOrtho monitors your aircraft's position, heading, and speed to predict which tiles you'll need next and downloads them in advance.

Prefetch is intentionally disabled while X-Plane displays the initial "Reading scenery files" screen. Live DDS requests receive all downloader and builder capacity until the parent process publishes a valid flight connection. After the flight starts, prefetch uses a separate bounded queue; live requests remain unbounded and always take priority.

How it works:

With SimBrief flight data loaded: 1. AutoOrtho follows your actual flight plan, interpolating between waypoints 2. Uses SimBrief's calculated times (accounting for winds and climb/descent) 3. Prioritizes tiles by time-to-encounter (closest tiles first) 4. Downloads tiles uniformly along your entire route

Without SimBrief (velocity-based): 1. AutoOrtho tracks your aircraft's heading and ground speed 2. It calculates which tiles are in your flight path ahead 3. It downloads those tiles in the background before you reach them

Prefetching with Dynamic Zoom:

When Dynamic Zoom is enabled, the prefetcher uses your predicted AGL altitude at each prefetch location to determine the appropriate zoom level. This means: - Tiles prefetched for a descent will be at higher zoom levels - Tiles prefetched for cruise will be at lower zoom levels - Each prefetched tile matches what you'll actually need when you get there

Recommendation: Keep enabled for the smoothest in-flight experience.

docs.title: Lookahead Time (prefetch_lookahead)
docs.text:
• Type: Integer (minutes)
  • Default: 10
  • Range: 1 - 60 minutes
  • Config file: prefetch_lookahead = 10

How far ahead (in minutes of flight time) to prefetch tiles.

Value At 150 kts At 300 kts At 500 kts Use Case 5 min ~12nm ~25nm ~42nm Conservative, less bandwidth 10 min ~25nm ~50nm ~83nm Balanced (default) 20 min ~50nm ~100nm ~166nm Longer flights, faster aircraft 30 min ~75nm ~150nm ~250nm Cross-country flights 60 min ~150nm ~300nm ~500nm Maximum prefetch coverage

Example: At 300 knots ground speed with 10 minute lookahead: - Distance: 300 kts × 10 min = 50 nautical miles ahead - AutoOrtho will prefetch tiles up to 50nm in front of you

Recommendation: - Short flights / GA: 5-10 minutes - Medium flights / Jets: 10-20 minutes - Long haul / Fast jets: 20-30 minutes

docs.title: Stutter-Free Flying (Prioritize Performance)
docs.text:
band_max_wait_seconds = 4.0
fallback_level = cache
fallback_extends_budget = False
prefetch_enabled = True
prefetch_lookahead = 30
max_zoom_level = 16

docs.title: Maximum Quality (Prioritize Imagery)
docs.text:
band_max_wait_seconds = 10.0
near_wait_seconds = 120.0
fallback_level = full
fallback_extends_budget = True
prefetch_enabled = True
prefetch_lookahead = 60
max_zoom_level = 17

docs.title: Slow Internet Connection
docs.text:
band_max_wait_seconds = 8.0
fallback_level = cache
fallback_extends_budget = False
prefetch_enabled = True
prefetch_lookahead = 90
max_zoom_level = 16

docs.title: Weak CPU / Limited System
docs.text:
band_max_wait_seconds = 6.0
fallback_level = none
fallback_extends_budget = False
prefetch_enabled = False
max_zoom_level = 15

docs.title: Understanding the Statistics
docs.text:
AutoOrtho logs performance statistics that can help you tune your settings:

STATS: {'mm_count:0': 12, 'mm_count:1': 26, 'chunk_budget_skipped': 8782, 'chunk_missing_count': 394}

docs.title: Key Statistics
docs.text:
Statistic Meaning mm_count:N Successful mipmap builds at level N (0=highest detail) chunk_budget_skipped Chunks skipped because time budget ran out chunk_missing_count Chunks that ended up with missing color (no fallback worked)

Healthy indicators: - High mm_count:0 values = high-detail tiles completing successfully - Low chunk_missing_count = fallbacks working well

Warning signs: - High chunk_budget_skipped = many chunks timing out, raise Wait for nearby imagery in flight (band_max_wait_seconds) - High chunk_missing_count = fallbacks not covering gaps, enable more fallbacks

docs.title: Breaking Down Tile Creation Time
docs.text:
Each tile creation has two main phases:

  1. Download + Compose (typically 60-80% of time)
  2. Downloading 64-4096 image chunks (depending on zoom level)
  3. Decoding JPEG data

  4. Compositing into a single image

  5. Compression (typically 20-40% of time)

  6. Converting RGBA to DDS format
  7. Generating mipmaps

The stats show both the total time and compression-only time, letting you identify bottlenecks: - If compression time is high → CPU-bound, consider lowering zoom level - If download time is high → Network-bound, check internet speed

docs.title: Time-Based Exclusion
docs.text: AutoOrtho includes a time-based exclusion feature that allows you to automatically disable AutoOrtho scenery during specific time ranges in the simulator. This is useful for night flying when satellite imagery provides little benefit.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
When time exclusion is active:

  1. AutoOrtho monitors the simulator's local time via the sim/time/local_time_sec dataref
  2. During the exclusion period, DSF file reads are redirected to X-Plane's global scenery
  3. X-Plane uses its default scenery (which often has better night lighting)
  4. When the exclusion period ends, AutoOrtho scenery becomes available again

Important: DSF files are never hidden from X-Plane. X-Plane indexes DSF files at flight load time, so hiding them would cause missing terrain. Instead, AutoOrtho redirects reads to the corresponding global scenery DSF files, ensuring terrain data is always available.

docs.title: Safety Features
docs.text:
The time exclusion system includes important safety features:

  • Active DSF Protection: DSF files that are currently in use by X-Plane will NOT be redirected, even if the exclusion period starts. This prevents crashes or graphical glitches.
  • Gradual Transition: Only new DSF requests are redirected during exclusion. Previously loaded scenery continues to work until X-Plane naturally releases it.
  • Global Scenery Fallback: When redirecting, AutoOrtho looks for the equivalent DSF in X-Plane's Global Scenery folder. If not found, the original AutoOrtho file is served.

docs.title: Enable Time Exclusion (enabled)
docs.text:
• Type: Boolean (True/False)
  • Default: False
  • Config file: [time_exclusion] section, enabled = True

Enable or disable the time-based exclusion feature.

docs.title: Start Time (start_time)
docs.text:
• Type: String (HH:MM format)
  • Default: 22:00
  • Config file: start_time = 22:00

The time when the exclusion period begins (24-hour format). For example, "22:00" for 10 PM.

docs.title: End Time (end_time)
docs.text:
• Type: String (HH:MM format)
  • Default: 06:00
  • Config file: end_time = 06:00

The time when the exclusion period ends (24-hour format). For example, "06:00" for 6 AM.

docs.title: Default to Exclusion (default_to_exclusion)
docs.text:
• Type: Boolean (True/False)
  • Default: False
  • Config file: default_to_exclusion = False

Controls behavior when sim time is not yet available (before flight starts):

Setting Behavior False (default) AutoOrtho works normally until sim time confirms exclusion True Assume exclusion is active until sim time proves otherwise

When to enable: - You want night flights to start with default scenery from the very beginning - You don't want any AutoOrtho scenery loaded before sim time is available

When to keep disabled: - You prefer AutoOrtho to work normally during loading screens - You only want exclusion to apply when sim time is confirmed

docs.title: Decision Preservation During Scenery Reload
docs.text:
Once the simulator time becomes available and AutoOrtho determines the correct exclusion state, this decision is preserved during temporary disconnections such as when you trigger "Reload Scenery" in X-Plane.

Why this matters:

Without decision preservation, the following problem would occur: 1. You start a flight with "Default to Exclusion" enabled 2. Time exclusion activates initially (no sim time available yet) 3. Sim time becomes available (e.g., 15:00 / 3 PM) → exclusion deactivates correctly 4. You trigger "Reload Scenery" in X-Plane 5. During reload, sim time temporarily becomes unavailable 6. ❌ Without preservation: exclusion would incorrectly re-activate 7. ✅ With preservation: exclusion stays inactive (correct behavior)

How it works:

  • When sim time is received, AutoOrtho records both the time and the exclusion decision
  • If sim time becomes temporarily unavailable (during reload), the last decision is preserved
  • The preserved decision is updated whenever new sim time data is received
  • Normal time-based transitions still work (crossing into/out of exclusion hours)

Limitations:

Limitation Description Persists until restart The preserved decision remains until AutoOrtho is fully restarted To reset behavior Quit and restart AutoOrtho to return to the default_to_exclusion initial behavior Updates on new time If sim time indicates a state change (e.g., crossing into night), it will update when time becomes available again

💡 Tip: If you notice the exclusion state is "stuck" after multiple scenery reloads, simply restart AutoOrtho to reset to the configured default behavior.

docs.title: Example Configuration
docs.text:
To disable AutoOrtho between 10 PM and 6 AM (night hours):

[time_exclusion]
enabled = True
start_time = 22:00
end_time = 06:00
default_to_exclusion = False

To ensure exclusion is active from the moment AutoOrtho starts (before sim time is available):

[time_exclusion]
enabled = True
start_time = 22:00
end_time = 06:00
default_to_exclusion = True

docs.title: Overnight Ranges
docs.text:
The system correctly handles overnight time ranges. For example, if you set: - Start: 22:00 (10 PM) - End: 06:00 (6 AM)

AutoOrtho will be disabled from 10 PM until 6 AM the next morning.

docs.title: UI Configuration
docs.text:
You can configure time exclusion in the AutoOrtho Settings tab:

  1. Go to Settings tab
  2. Find the Time Exclusion Settings group
  3. Check Enable time-based exclusion
  4. Set the Start time and End time in HH:MM format

docs.title: Use Cases
docs.text:
• Night Flying: Satellite imagery is often dark or less useful at night. Default X-Plane scenery may have better night lighting.
  • Performance Optimization: Reduce network usage and CPU load during night hours when visual quality matters less.
  • Dawn/Dusk Flying: Exclude twilight hours when satellite imagery transitions may look unrealistic.

docs.title: SimBrief Integration
docs.text: AutoOrtho can integrate with SimBrief to enhance Dynamic Zoom and Prefetching using your actual flight plan data. This provides more accurate predictions than velocity-based calculations alone.

docs.title: Setting Up SimBrief Integration
docs.text:
1. Go to Settings → Setup tab
  2. Find the SimBrief Integration section
  3. Enter your SimBrief User ID (found in your SimBrief account settings)
  4. Click Fetch Flight Data after filing your flight plan in SimBrief
  5. Enable Use Flight Data for Dynamic Zoom Level and Pre-fetching Calculations

Note: You can load SimBrief flight data at any time — before or after clicking Start Streaming. The toggle takes effect immediately, so you don't need to restart AutoOrtho or save the config when loading a flight plan mid-session.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text: When SimBrief integration is enabled and flight data is loaded:

docs.title: Dynamic Zoom with SimBrief
docs.text:
Instead of predicting altitude based on current vertical speed, AutoOrtho uses your planned altitudes from SimBrief:

  1. For each tile, finds the closest waypoint(s) in your flight plan
  2. Uses the planned AGL altitude at those waypoints
  3. If multiple waypoints are within the consideration radius (default 50nm), uses the lowest AGL altitude for conservative quality

Conservative AGL Calculation: - Uses the lowest flight altitude (MSL) among nearby waypoints — accounts for descents - Uses the highest ground elevation — accounts for mountains - AGL = lowest_MSL - highest_ground = most conservative (highest quality) result

docs.title: Prefetching with SimBrief
docs.text:
Instead of prefetching based on velocity vector prediction, AutoOrtho follows your actual flight path with time-based prioritization:

  1. Projects your position onto the route — finds exactly where you are on the flight plan
  2. Calculates your "current time" — interpolates between waypoint times based on position
  3. Walks forward along the entire path — interpolating between waypoints at regular intervals (not just around waypoints)
  4. Uses SimBrief's planned times — accounts for winds, climb/descent speeds, and holds
  5. Calculates time-to-encounter for each point along the path
  6. Prioritizes tiles by time — tiles you'll reach sooner are prefetched first
  7. Stops at the configured lookahead time — doesn't waste bandwidth on distant tiles

Key advantage: The path is uniformly sampled between waypoints, so even long oceanic legs or direct routes with distant waypoints get full coverage. Tiles are downloaded in the order you'll actually encounter them.

Example: If your next waypoint is 200nm away but you'll pass near a tile in 5 minutes, that tile is prefetched before tiles near the waypoint itself.

docs.title: Configuration Options
docs.text:
These settings are available under Flight Plan & Map → SimBrief Integration when flight data is loaded and the "Use Flight Data" toggle is enabled.

Setting Default Range Description Route Consideration Radius 50 nm 10-200 nm Radius around a tile to consider waypoints for altitude calculation. Uses the lowest altitude among nearby waypoints for conservative zoom level selection. Route Deviation Threshold 40 nm 5-100 nm Maximum distance off-route before falling back to DataRef-based calculations. Accounts for ATC vectors or weather avoidance. Route Prefetch Radius 40 nm 10-150 nm Radius around path points for pre-fetching tiles. Larger values prefetch more tiles perpendicular to your route.

ℹ Real-time Changes: All route settings take effect immediately when modified — no restart required. However, use Apply to persist your values for future AutoOrtho sessions.

docs.title: Fallback Behavior
docs.text:
SimBrief integration gracefully falls back to DataRef-based calculations when:

  1. No flight data loaded: Use velocity-based prediction from X-Plane DataRefs
  2. Aircraft off-route: If you deviate more than 40nm from the planned route, AutoOrtho assumes you're no longer following the plan and falls back to DataRef calculations
  3. DataRefs unavailable: If X-Plane isn't sending data yet, uses the base quality step (0ft AGL = maximum quality)

docs.title: Option A: Load flight plan before starting
docs.text:
1. File flight plan in SimBrief (e.g., KJFK → KLAX)
  2. Start AutoOrtho and go to Flight Plan & Map
  3. Enter SimBrief User ID and click "Fetch Flight Data"
  4. Verify flight info displays correctly (route, cruise altitude, aircraft)
  5. Enable toggle "Use Flight Data for Dynamic Zoom..."
  6. Click Start Streaming — AutoOrtho starts and begins prefetching along your route
  7. Start X-Plane and fly your route

docs.title: Option B: Load flight plan after starting (mid-session)
docs.text:
1. Start AutoOrtho and click Start Streaming (with your SimBrief User ID already saved)
  2. Start X-Plane and begin your flight
  3. File flight plan in SimBrief when ready
  4. Go to Flight Plan & Map and click Fetch Flight Data
  5. Enable toggle — takes effect immediately, no restart needed
  6. AutoOrtho will immediately start using your flight plan for prefetching and dynamic zoom

docs.title: Zoom Level Transitions
docs.text:
When flying through areas where the zoom level changes (e.g., from ZL16 to ZL15 during climb), you may notice:

  • Hard visual transitions: Adjacent tiles at different zoom levels may have visible seams due to:
  • Different imagery capture dates
  • Different color processing/calibration

  • Resolution differences at tile boundaries

  • Color mismatches: Satellite imagery from different zoom levels is often captured at different times, so colors, seasons, and lighting may not match perfectly.

Mitigation strategies: - Configure fewer, larger altitude steps to reduce the number of transitions - Accept some quality variation for the performance benefits - Use similar zoom levels for adjacent altitude ranges (e.g., ZL16/ZL16 instead of ZL16/ZL14)

docs.title: SimBrief Integration Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Description Single flight plan Only the most recently fetched SimBrief flight plan is used. Multi-leg flights require re-fetching between legs. Static ground heights Ground elevation data comes from SimBrief's database, which may differ slightly from X-Plane's terrain. Route deviation detection The 40nm off-route threshold is a straight-line distance, not a cross-track distance. Complex routes near waypoints may trigger false positives. No automatic refresh Flight data is fetched once when you click the button. Changes to your SimBrief flight plan require manual re-fetch. Holding patterns SimBrief fixes don't include holding patterns. If you hold, AutoOrtho may use incorrect altitude predictions.

docs.title: DataRef-Based Prediction Limitations
docs.text:
When not using SimBrief (or when off-route), altitude prediction uses X-Plane DataRefs:

Limitation Description Vertical speed extrapolation Assumes current vertical speed will continue, which may not be accurate for complex climb/descent profiles. 60-second averaging window Predictions are based on a 60-second rolling average, so rapid changes in flight path take time to reflect. No terrain awareness DataRef-based predictions use current AGL but don't know about upcoming terrain changes.

docs.title: Prefetching Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Description Priority system Prefetched tiles are always lower priority than tiles X-Plane directly requests. During rapid maneuvering, prefetching pauses. Network-dependent Prefetching requires available network bandwidth. On slow connections, prefetching may not keep up with fast aircraft. Cache eviction Prefetched tiles can be evicted from cache if memory limits are reached before you reach those tiles.

docs.title: General Limitations
docs.text: Limitation Description Imagery availability Not all zoom levels are available in all areas. Some regions only have imagery up to ZL15 or ZL16. Server-side rate limiting Excessive requests may be throttled by imagery providers, affecting both real-time and prefetch downloads. Memory usage Higher zoom levels and extensive prefetching increase memory usage. Monitor system RAM on limited systems.

docs.title: Native Pipeline Architecture
docs.text: AutoOrtho includes a high-performance native pipeline (aopipeline) written in C that bypasses Python's Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) for CPU-intensive operations. This provides 10-20x faster DDS texture building compared to the Python-only path.

docs.title: Why Native Code?
docs.text:
Python's GIL (Global Interpreter Lock) prevents true multi-threading for CPU-bound work. Even with multiple Python threads, only one can execute Python bytecode at a time. This caused stutters when multiple DDS textures needed to be built simultaneously.

The native pipeline solves this by: 1. Moving CPU-intensive work entirely to C code 2. Using OpenMP for true parallel execution across all CPU cores 3. Calling into Python only for orchestration, not computation

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The native pipeline consists of four modules:

Module Purpose Parallelism AoCache Batch file I/O for cached JPEGs OpenMP parallel reads AoDecode JPEG decoding via TurboJPEG OpenMP parallel decodes AoDDS DDS texture building with ISPC compression OpenMP parallel compression AoHttp HTTP downloads via libcurl Connection pooling, HTTP/2

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
When X-Plane requests a tile, AutoOrtho's native pipeline:

  1. Batch reads all cached JPEG chunks in parallel (256 files for ZL16)
  2. Batch decodes all JPEGs using thread-local TurboJPEG handles
  3. Composes the full tile image using SIMD-optimized operations
  4. Compresses each DDS mipmap level in parallel using ISPC
  5. Returns the complete DDS to Python for serving to X-Plane

All steps happen in native C threads, completely bypassing the Python GIL.

docs.title: Performance Impact
docs.text: Metric Python-Only Native Pipeline Improvement Cache read (256 files) 500ms 50ms 10x JPEG decode (256 chunks) 800ms 100ms 8x DDS compression 1000ms 80ms 12x Total tile build 2.5s ~260ms ~10x

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
[autoortho]
# Maximum threads per native build (0 = auto, divided across concurrent builds)
# Set to 1 for single-threaded mode (lowest CPU, slowest builds)
native_pipeline_threads = 0

# Early-build threshold: start DDS build when this fraction of chunks are ready (0.5-1.0)
# 1.0 = wait for all chunks (single build, no placeholders)
# 0.9 = build at 90%, automatically rebuild when remaining 10% arrive
live_aopipeline_min_chunk_ratio = 1.0

# Persistent compiled DDS cache size in MB.
# 0 delegates retention to the shared disk budget.
persistent_dds_cache_mb = 0

The persistent DDS cache is implemented by DynamicDDSCache. When its independent limit is 0, file_cache_size remains the overall disk limit and dds_budget_pct is the literal DDS share; JPEG source files receive the remainder. DDS data, DDM metadata, and partial-row sidecars are all included in that accounting.

docs.title: Thread Configuration
docs.text: Value Behavior 0 (default) Auto: divides CPU cores across concurrent builds to avoid oversubscription 1 Single-threaded (useful for debugging or very low-end CPUs) N Fixed N threads per build (regardless of concurrent build count)

docs.title: Early-Build Threshold (live_aopipeline_min_chunk_ratio)
docs.text:
Controls a two-phase build strategy that trades brief placeholder artifacts for faster first texture appearance:

Phase 1 — Early build: fires as soon as this ratio of chunks is available. Any missing chunks are filled with the missing color.

Phase 2 — Healing pass: fires automatically when the remaining chunks arrive, replacing placeholder areas with real imagery.

Value Behavior 1.0 (default) Wait for all chunks — single build, no placeholders, no healing needed 0.9 Build at 90% — texture appears ~10% sooner, healed silently after 0.8 Build at 80% — texture appears earlier, more placeholder area to heal

At 1.0 there is no behavioral difference from before — the tile only builds once all chunks are present. Values below 1.0 are useful on slow connections where waiting for the last few chunks causes noticeable delay before a tile becomes visible.

docs.title: Ephemeral DDS Cache
docs.text:
The native pipeline includes an ephemeral disk cache for pre-built DDS textures:

  • Memory tier: Fast access for recently used tiles (configurable, default 512MB)
  • Disk tier: Overflow storage in temp directory (configurable, default 4GB)
  • Auto-cleanup: Disk cache is deleted when AutoOrtho exits

This hybrid approach provides: - ✅ Large cache capacity without permanent disk usage - ✅ Fresh tiles every session (no stale/corrupted cache) - ✅ Settings changes take effect immediately (no cache invalidation needed)

docs.title: Native HTTP Client
docs.text:
The native HTTP client uses libcurl's multi-interface for high-performance chunk downloads:

Feature Benefit Connection pooling Reuses TCP connections across requests HTTP/2 multiplexing Multiple requests over single connection Batch processing Amortizes Python overhead across 64 chunks Parallel downloads True concurrent I/O, not GIL-limited

This is especially impactful during initial loading when 100,000+ chunk requests are queued.

docs.title: Apple Maps Fallback
docs.text:
Apple Maps (APPLE imagery source) uses the shared Python HTTP/2 broker, not the native libcurl client. This preserves:

  1. Dynamic token: Apple requires a session-specific access token obtained via DuckDuckGo proxy
  2. Token rotation: On 403/410 errors, the token must be refreshed and the request retried
  3. Complex logic: The Python path handles all this special authentication flow

Impact: Apple Maps downloads may be slightly slower than other sources, but all retry logic and token handling works correctly.

# Native HTTP path (fast):
BI, EOX, ARC, NAIP, USGS, FIREFLY, YNDX, GO2 → libcurl → parallel downloads

# Shared broker path (full features):
APPLE → asynchronous HTTP/2 broker → token rotation on 403/410

docs.title: Platform Support
docs.text:
The native pipeline requires compiled libraries for each platform:

Platform Library Status macOS (ARM64) libaopipeline.dylib ✅ Included macOS (x86_64) libaopipeline.dylib Build from source Linux (x64) libaopipeline.so Build from source Windows (x64) aopipeline.dll Build from source

If the native library is not available for your platform, AutoOrtho automatically falls back to the Python implementation.

docs.title: Fallback Behavior
docs.text:
The native pipeline gracefully falls back to Python when: - Native library is not available or fails to load - Apple Maps source is used (token handling) - Transient HTTP errors need sophisticated retry logic - Chunk downloads fail and need server rotation

You'll see log messages indicating which path is used:

INFO: Using NativeChunkGetter (32 connections)
INFO: Native HTTP client available: 1.0.0

Or for fallback:

INFO: Using Python ChunkGetter (32 workers)
DEBUG: Native HTTP client library not available, using Python requests fallback

docs.title: Long X-Plane Loading Times
docs.text:
If X-Plane takes significantly longer to load scenery with AutoOrtho enabled, the most common cause is the wait while a flight loads (near_wait_seconds, 60 s): nearby textures wait that long for real imagery, and before X-Plane first connects a tile may take ten times its normal budget.

To reduce loading times:

  1. Go to Settings → Streaming
  2. Lower "Wait while a flight loads", for example to 20 seconds
  3. Nearby textures then wait less during the loading screen, resulting in faster loads

Note: X-Plane does not automatically refresh a texture after consuming it. Choose the startup budget and fallback policy according to the quality required for the initial load; background healing improves only future cache reads.

docs.title: Other Common Issues
docs.text: See the FAQ for common issues related to: - Missing color (green) tiles - Long loading times - In-flight stuttering

docs.title: Using provided sceneries
docs.text:
IMPORTANT

Use Scenery Library to search, filter, install, update, and remove regions. AutoOrtho checks the destination and temporary-download folders before an installation begins, shows the expected storage requirement, and blocks the operation when the destination is not writable or space is clearly insufficient.

Installations and patch operations remain visible in the Activity panel while you navigate elsewhere. A cancelled operation stops at a safe boundary; AutoOrtho either preserves resumable download data or cleans incomplete output. Completed and failed operations remain visible until dismissed, and failures offer the recovery actions that are safe for that operation.

The scenery packs provided with this tool that you download should be setup via the configuration utility. This does more than simply download and extract the files.

If you do wish to manually manipulate these scenery packs, you should review the source code (downloader.py in particular) and understand how symlinks and/or junctions work and the limitations of each.

If you manually move things around outside of the configuration utility, things very well might break!

IMPORTANT

docs.title: Streaming scenery instead of installing regions
docs.text:
You don't have to download whole regions before you fly. With scenery streaming on, AutoOrtho downloads each 1x1 degree tile the first time X-Plane needs it, from the same GitHub releases the region installer uses.

Only the tile's base mesh is downloaded: its DSF file and water masks, typically about 3 MB per tile and up to about 15 MB for detailed ones. The terrain files are generated on the fly, and satellite imagery is fetched as usual.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
On a new installation, the setup wizard offers streaming on its Scenery step: tick Stream scenery you haven't installed and pick the same settings as below. You can stream instead of installing regions, or as well. See First-run setup.

To turn it on later:

  1. Stop AutoOrtho if it's running. Streaming settings are locked while AutoOrtho or X-Plane is running.
  2. Open Scenery Library. The Stream scenery panel is at the top.
  3. Pick the Scenery set:
  4. XP11 legacy set (kubilus1/autoortho-scenery): the same meshes as the regions offered in the Scenery Library.
  5. XP12 set: coming soon. It's marked Soon until its packages are ready for streaming.
  6. Choose whether to Include overlays (roads, forests, buildings). See Overlays and simHeaven.
  7. Set the Disk limit (20 GB by default).
  8. Tick Stream scenery you haven't installed. AutoOrtho downloads the tile index, a few megabytes, and sets up the streaming folders.
  9. Start AutoOrtho, then X-Plane.

You can change the scenery set, overlays and disk limit at any time while AutoOrtho is stopped. Changes are applied right away, whether streaming is on or off, and take effect the next time AutoOrtho starts. AutoOrtho asks first when a change would delete tiles you've already streamed.

docs.title: Installed regions always come first
docs.text:
Streaming only covers tiles you haven't installed. If a region is installed, X-Plane uses its tiles and streaming fills in the rest of the world. That means you can:

  • Stream everything and install nothing.
  • Install the regions you fly most and stream the rest. Installed tiles load without waiting for a download, and you can fly them offline.

To stream a region you have installed, uninstall it from the Scenery Library.

docs.title: Overlays and simHeaven
docs.text:
If you use simHeaven X-World or another overlay package, turn Include overlays off. simHeaven already provides roads, forests and buildings, so streaming AutoOrtho's overlays as well would duplicate them.

With overlays on, AutoOrtho streams the overlays that come with the scenery set. If you still have the classic Custom Scenery/yAutoOrtho_Overlays folder, its tiles are used instead of streamed ones, even when it's disabled in scenery_packs.ini. To stream overlays instead, move that folder out of Custom Scenery.

docs.title: Disk use
docs.text:
Streamed tiles stay on disk, so each tile is downloaded only once. When the stored tiles grow past the disk limit, AutoOrtho removes the tiles you haven't used for the longest time, down to 90% of the limit.

  • Tiles used in the last two hours are never removed.
  • Tiles you keep for offline flying are never removed and don't count toward the limit.
  • Overlays get a quarter of the limit on top of it. With a 20 GB limit, overlays can use another 5 GB.
  • The panel shows how many tiles are stored and how much space they use. The disk limit covers only the base mesh. Satellite imagery has its own cache limit in Settings.

docs.title: When you fly
docs.text:
• When X-Plane opens a tile, AutoOrtho downloads it and the tiles around it. The first flight in a new area takes longer to load. Later flights there load at normal speed.
  • If a tile can't be downloaded (no connection, or GitHub is unavailable), X-Plane gets the tile from its default Global Scenery instead, so you see default terrain there rather than an error. A missing overlay tile is served empty, and a missing water mask is served blank, which shows X-Plane's default water along that stretch of coast until the scenery reloads.
  • Dropped connections are retried straight away, so a hiccup costs a second or two rather than a fallback.
  • If GitHub throttles downloads, AutoOrtho pauses downloads (from one minute up to 15 minutes) and then tries again. Tiles needed during the pause come from Global Scenery.
  • Downloaded tile indexes are checked for updates once a week.

docs.title: Where the files are
docs.text:
Streaming creates these folders next to your installed regions in Custom Scenery/z_autoortho/scenery/:

  • z_ao_stream_xp11: the streamed base mesh.
  • yAO_stream_xp11_overlays: the streamed overlays, if you included them.

Like installed regions, each one appears in Custom Scenery while AutoOrtho is running. Don't edit or move these folders yourself; use the Stream scenery panel.

When AutoOrtho starts, it adds the streaming folders to scenery_packs.ini and keeps the streamed overlays above the AutoOrtho base meshes. The first time it changes the file, it keeps your original as scenery_packs.ini.ao_backup.

docs.title: Seeing and managing stored tiles on the map
docs.text:
Flight Plan & Map has a map with two views. Switch with the buttons above the map:

  • Imagery Sources: the Custom Map editor, which picks the imagery source per tile.
  • Cache: what AutoOrtho has stored for each 1x1 degree tile.

In the Cache view, tiles are coloured by what's stored: Streamed scenery (base mesh, overlays and water masks), Imagery (cached satellite imagery), or Both. Choose Colour by: Size to colour them by how much space they use instead. A white outline marks tiles kept for offline flying. Hover over a tile to see its sizes, imagery zoom levels and sources, and when it was last used. The line under the map shows the totals.

To select tiles, click one or drag a box. Hold Ctrl or Shift to add to the selection, or to remove a tile you click. Press Esc to clear it. More has Select Stored Tiles in View and Zoom to Stored Tiles.

Deleting tiles and keeping them offline only work while AutoOrtho and X-Plane are stopped, like the streaming settings. You can look at the map at any time.

docs.title: Deleting stored tiles
docs.text:
Select tiles, then choose Delete > Streamed Scenery, Imagery or Both. AutoOrtho shows how much it's about to delete and asks first.

  • Deleted streamed scenery is downloaded again the next time you fly there, so you need an internet connection then. Deleting it also stops keeping the tile for offline flying.
  • Deleted imagery is downloaded again when X-Plane needs it.
  • Installed regions aren't affected. Only streamed tiles and cached imagery are deleted.

docs.title: Keeping tiles for offline flying
docs.text:
Select tiles, then click Keep Offline. AutoOrtho shows how much streamed scenery it will download, then downloads each tile's DSF and water masks (and overlays, if you stream them) right away. Progress shows in the Activity panel, where you can cancel it. Kept tiles are never removed to make room.

The confirmation also estimates how much space the imagery for those tiles would take at ZL16, ZL17 and ZL18. Keep Offline doesn't download imagery. To fly a kept area offline with satellite imagery, fly it once with a connection so its imagery is cached, and make sure the imagery cache limit in Settings is large enough to hold it.

To stop keeping tiles, select them and choose Keep Offline > Stop Keeping. Their files stay on disk until the disk limit needs the space.

Tiles with no streamed scenery, such as open water, are skipped.

docs.title: Turning it off
docs.text: Untick Stream scenery you haven't installed. AutoOrtho asks before deleting the tiles streamed so far. Installed regions aren't affected.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Scenery Patches (Seasons, Terrain reflectivity) are applied only to installed regions, not to streamed tiles yet.
  • Keep Offline keeps only the streamed scenery. Imagery isn't downloaded ahead of time; it's cached as you fly.
  • The setup wizard only turns streaming on. To change its settings or turn it off afterwards, use the Scenery Library.

docs.title: Configuring scenery_packs.ini
docs.text:
Any scenery added to XPlane requires being setup in the scenery_packs.ini file located in your installs 'Custom Scenery' directory.

This file is order dependent where higher priority layers are towards the top of the file and lower priority items are towards the bottom.

On initial run of XPlane after installing new scenery, these layers will automatically be added to your scenery_packs.ini file, but likely in an incorrect location.

This can result in strange issues, such as having no roads, buildings, or trees when flying with XPlane. If this is the case, double check the order of files in scenery_packs.ini.

This tool will download and setup numerous directories in your 'Custom Scenery' folder of the form: z_ao_<short name of scenery pack> and a directory named yAutoOrtho_Overlays. Typically these should be listed towards the bottom of your scenery_packs.ini file:

Landmarks, airports, etc
simHeaven, special layers, etc
yAutoOrtho_Overlays
yAO_stream_xp11_overlays
z_ao_aus_pac
z_ao_eur
z_ao_na
z_ao_stream_xp11
z_autoortho
zzz_global_scenery

yAO_stream_xp11_overlays and z_ao_stream_xp11 appear only if scenery streaming is on. AutoOrtho places them for you when it starts.

docs.title: Installing in custom directories
docs.text:
It is possible to install scenery into directories other than X-Plane's Custom Scenery directory.

You should have a good understanding of how X-Plane handles custom scenery before attempting this!

  1. This will require that you configure AutoOrtho to point the 'Custom Scenery' setting to this alternative directory.
  2. Setup and install scenery as per normal. Run the program at least once to create the mount points. You should see folder that correspond to the installed packages now in the alternative directory that was setup. The format will look like z_ao_XXXX
  3. You will then need to manually link each of the resulting mount directories to X-Planes's origin Custom Scenery dir. On Linux you can use a symlink. On Windows you can create a shortcut.
  4. Make sure Autoortho is running and start X-Plane. Double check your scenery_packs.ini file to assure the directories are seen.

docs.title: Windows native crash diagnostics
docs.text:
For macOS and Linux, see Native crash diagnostics.

Windows builds start the bundled ao-crash-collector.exe automatically for each mount worker. It attaches before that worker imports native extensions. The reporter starts AutoOrtho and flies as usual; no ProcDump installation, registry edits, administrator privileges or configuration changes are needed under normal same-user process permissions.

The collector passes first-chance exceptions back to the application. On an unhandled native exception (including Windows fast-fail 0xC0000409), it writes diagnostics while the worker is stopped, then lets Windows terminate the worker with its original exception code. Normal worker exits do not produce dumps. A collector failure releases the startup gate, and its exit does not kill a worker. The gate has a 15-second fallback timeout. Attach failures are recorded in the worker log and streaming can continue without crash capture.

Files are stored locally in %USERPROFILE%\.autoortho-data\crashes:

  • worker-<pid>-<id>.dmp: native thread stacks, exception context, module list and memory referenced by stacks (not a full worker heap dump).
  • .crash.json: exception code, address, thread ID, exception parameters (parameter zero is the fast-fail subcode), and dump/context errors if any.
  • .modules.jsonl: actual loaded module paths and base addresses.
  • .build.json: build revision, source hashes and native artifact hashes.
  • .complete: indicates that the collector finished writing the bundle.

The latest three completed bundles are retained when another worker starts; active collectors are not pruned. Nothing is uploaded automatically. Dumps can contain paths and memory holding private data; share a bundle privately with a maintainer rather than attaching it to a public issue. Existing worker logs are in %USERPROFILE%\.autoortho-data\logs.

docs.title: Building and verifying
docs.text:
The windows-native.yml workflow cross-compiles the pipeline and collector from the current checkout, records hashes in native-build.json, and runs Windows checks for fast-fail capture, handled exceptions, normal exit and collector exit.
